  • ⚠ The imagery is the 07-28 development, not the attack. The strikes were claimed around 07-21. Recorded as corroboration of an older event — the distinction matters because the campaign, not the incident, is what this thread tracks.
  • Landed the same day Iran struck a US base in Jordan (5:45pm ET, all intercepted) — the first ballistic-missile attack on a US base since the 07-24 pause. Compute infrastructure and conventional military targets in the same 24 hours. The recall lesson is logged in coverage-log.md.

headline: A further drone strike on Amazon in Bahrain
html: • An Iranian drone struck an Amazon data centre in Bahrain (FT).

headline: Iran names its corporate target list
html: • Iranian state media said it would target American companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple, Meta, Oracle, Intel, HP, IBM, Cisco, Dell, Palantir and Nvidia — the declaration that turns individual strikes into a stated campaign.

headline: The first strikes: AWS sites in the UAE
html: • Before dawn, Iranian Shahed drones struck two Amazon Web Services data centres in the United Arab Emirates; a third commercial data centre in Bahrain was hit, though whether it was deliberately targeted is less clear. Reported as the first time a country has deliberately targeted commercial data centres in wartime.

headline: DeepMind's new chief says Gemini 4 is nearing release
html: • Google DeepMind's new chief, Koray Kavukcuoglu, said Gemini 4 is nearing release and that Google aims to ship an early post-training version "much earlier" than the end of the year In his first media interview as DeepMind's leader, given to The Information, he conceded Google "took a little bit of a step back" to ship faster Flash models instead of the Gemini 3.5 Pro update promised for June. (The Information, The Verge)

headline: DeepMind launches an AGI-focused institute, with Hassabis's new chairman title doing real work
html: • Google DeepMind launched the "DeepMind Institute" on Wednesday 09-16, an AGI-focused research and policy body listing DeepMind co-founder Shane Legg as managing editor and Google SVP James Manyika and DeepMind Chair Demis Hassabis as directors. The institute's stated aim is to surface differing views between Google, DeepMind, and the wider research community on AGI's societal impact — "they will not always agree, and they will likely change their minds," its founding announcement said. Its inaugural essays cover economic policy for AGI disruption, keeping model reasoning human-readable, and a framework for evaluating frontier models that would start by consulting AI companies but move toward independent, undisclosed "held-out" tests; Hassabis said the framework could be "ratcheted up if the seriousness of the situation demands," up to and including a coordinated slowdown among frontier developers. This is the most concrete evidence yet of what Hassabis's post-CEO "chairman and Chief Scientist" role actually does — publishing and speaking through a body he now chairs, rather than an honorary title, directly answering this thread's own open watch question. (TechCrunch, Axios, original)

headline: Discovery Loop's valuation quintuples to ~$50B in weeks, and its business is now known: parallel AI experiments for science
html: • Jeff Dean's AI-for-science startup Discovery Loop is raising a new funding round targeting roughly a $50 billion valuation, per Business Insider — up from about $10 billion "just weeks" earlier, when it raised roughly $1 billion. Reported 2026-09-11, corroborated the same week by Tech Funding News and multiple financial aggregators (Investing.com, KuCoin, PANews). This is the first hard answer to this thread's own open watch item, "what Discovery Loop builds": the company, co-founded by Dean with fellow ex-Google Brain/DeepMind veterans Sanjay Ghemawat, Quoc Le and Oriol Vinyals, aims to use AI to run thousands of experiments in parallel to accelerate scientific and engineering research. Terms remain unconfirmed and could still change — this is a target valuation for an in-progress round, not a closed deal. (Tech Funding News, citing Business Insider, KuCoin)

sources.label: Tech Funding News, citing Business Insider

headline: DeepMind's new operational chief says frontier leadership is the only thing that matters, and admits the lab is currently behind
html: • Koray Kavukcuoglu, in his first substantive public interview since taking over Gemini/frontier research day-to-day (with Google engineer Logan Kilpatrick), said bluntly: "there's nothing other than being at the frontier that is important for us." He acknowledged current models are "a little bit below the frontier" but said the team has what it needs to close the gap, pointed to the Flash-series progression (3.5 through 3.7) as evidence of agentic progress, and revealed Gemini 3.5 Pro is running "months late." This is a direct, on-the-record answer to this thread's own open watch question — whether the Hassabis-to-Kavukcuoglu handover "reads as succession planning or a real strategy shift" — from the person now running the lab day to day. (the-decoder.com)

headline: The team built to evaluate AI's worst risks moves out of the lab and into lobbying
html:
• The Wall Street Journal reported (exclusive, 08-26, citing an internal email) that Google is moving its roughly 90-person "AI responsibility" team out of DeepMind and into Google's global-affairs organization — the group covering chemical/biological/radiological/nuclear (CBRN) risk, human-AI interaction, and chatbot psychological-impact research. A Google spokesperson framed it as consolidation: "By bringing our AI responsibility teams closer together we're strengthening their ability to inform safety for our models and products." Two unnamed DeepMind employees told the WSJ they worry the move will cut the team off from the model development it's meant to evaluate and weaken its independence. Widely corroborated 08-26→08-28 (PYMNTS, Quartz, DigiTimes, Android Headlines, Times Now, NewsBytes, Times of India, TipRanks), all tracing to the same WSJ story. (PYMNTS, citing WSJ)
  • This is a concrete answer to the thread's own open question. The 08-05 opening entry asked whether Kavukcuoglu's promotion "reads as succession planning or a real strategy shift." Moving the safety-evaluation function for the lab's most severe risk category (CBRN) out of the research organization entirely, three weeks into his tenure running it day-to-day, points toward "real shift." Cross-outlet coverage the same window (Fortune, Storyboard18, Adgully, Indian Television) also reports DeepMind's share of elite AI research talent declining against rivals — ⚠️ specific figures not retrieved, noted as directionally consistent context rather than a sourced finding.

headline: Barret Zoph arrives as VP of Research, into the function whose departures are being priced
html: • Barret Zoph joined Google DeepMind as VP of Research, working on Gemini's reinforcement-learning and post-training — the pipeline Koray Kavukcuoglu now runs day to day. The route back is unusual: Google Brain resident, Google researcher to 2022, OpenAI post-training lead, co-founder of Thinking Machines Lab with Mira Murati, pushed out by Murati in January over disputed "performance, conduct and trust issues", a five-month return to OpenAI, and now Google again. The reason it belongs on this thread rather than in a gossip column is the timing: this is senior inbound research talent arriving in the exact week Alphabet's ~$700bn drawdown is being attributed, by Bloomberg, to research departures including Jeff Dean's and Hassabis's own exit as DeepMind CEO. ⚠️ Neither a Google/DeepMind post nor Zoph's own statement could be retrieved directly; the report is TechCrunch's, with Reuters and WSJ in the same window. Thinking Machines has not commented. (TechCrunch)

headline: Market reacts; Hassabis's exit was a year in the making; Discovery Loop's founding team named
html:
• Alphabet/Google shares fell roughly 4-5% (~$160-200B in market cap) the day of the announcement — the clearest signal yet that markets read this as more than a ceremonial reshuffle, not just a title swap. (CNBC)
  • Hassabis had been quietly delegating CEO duties to Koray Kavukcuoglu for about a year before the announcement, per a Semafor exclusive — a gradual handover, not a sudden departure. Hassabis, in a note to staff: "now is the right time for me to hand over my day-to-day operational responsibilities at GDM, so that I have the time and space to focus on the big picture." He reportedly found more fulfillment, especially since winning the Nobel Prize in 2024, running Isomorphic Labs (Google's AI-drug-discovery spinout) than in day-to-day tech-executive duties — that's where he's said to be refocusing, alongside the new chairman/Chief-Scientist roles. (Semafor)
  • Kavukcuoglu's mandate is concrete: he now runs Gemini day-to-day, including the anticipated Gemini 4 model — this reads as a real operational handoff, answering one of this thread's open watch questions (it is succession with a real portfolio, not an honorary bump). (CNBC)
  • Discovery Loop's founding team is larger than first reported: Jeff Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals, and Quoc Le — four senior Google/DeepMind research leaders, not Dean alone. Structured as a public benefit corporation aiming to automate ML/science/engineering research, with Google as a founding investor and cloud partner. Framed internally as an amicable exit — Pichai reportedly expressed personal sadness at Dean's departure. (CNBC)
  • Competitive backdrop, per the same coverage: Google's AI models are reportedly running roughly 6 months behind frontier capability on coding — where the industry's compute race is currently concentrated — though no outlet has yet drawn a direct causal line from that gap to the timing of this transition. Worth watching as context, not yet a confirmed driver.

headline: Opened
html:
• Thread opened — a leadership reset at a top-3 frontier lab.
  • Hassabis steps down as DeepMind CEO; Jeff Dean leaves Google after 27 years. Demis Hassabis becomes DeepMind chairman and Alphabet's Chief Scientist; Koray Kavukcuoglu is promoted to SVP of DeepMind, reporting directly to Sundar Pichai. Separately, Jeff Dean — Google's longest-tenured engineering leader — is leaving to found "Discovery Loop," an AI-for-science startup that Google itself is backing. Confirmed via Pichai's own post. Unclear from initial coverage whether the CEO transition and Dean's departure are connected or coincide by timing. (Axios, CNBC)

headline: Pentagon announces an Autonomous Warfare Command
html:
• Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command to build and field drones, robots and other autonomous systems across the US military, the first new US command since Space Command in 2019 He said it will have powers similar to the services, be set up over several months and launch within a year, with an interim effort called Project Agincourt and new job specialties for operators of autonomous systems; he spoke at Quantico in his State of the Force speech. (The Straits Times, The Next Web)
  • Hegseth tapped Elon Musk, Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich to lead "Project Meridian," a 120-day review of the weapons, technologies and capabilities the US military will need in future wars He said the effort "is not about developing new strategies or new policies" but about identifying "the domains that we must conquer, and capabilities we must master"; CNBC notes that Musk's SpaceX and Luckey's Anduril both hold large Pentagon contracts. (CNBC, The Hill via Yahoo)

headline: A divided D.C. Circuit panel lets the Pentagon keep Anthropic designated a supply-chain risk
html: • A divided D.C. Circuit panel ruled 2-1 on Friday that the Pentagon may keep its second supply-chain-risk designation of Anthropic in place, so the block on Claude in defence systems can continue The majority wrote that the department "had ample support for its conclusion" that integrating Claude "presented a statutorily covered national-security risk," and rejected Anthropic's due-process and free-speech claims. Judge Rita Lin's August ruling against the other designation stands. Anthropic said it is "considering all options," which could include asking the full court or the Supreme Court to review it. (Wired)

headline: Pentagon investigators cite overreliance on Palantir's Maven in the Minab school strike
html: • Pentagon investigators found that flawed intelligence, outdated imagery, a compressed targeting timetable, cuts to civilian-protection staff and overreliance on the AI in Palantir's Maven Smart System contributed to the February 28 missile strike that killed at least 123 children at an elementary school in Minab, Iran, Bloomberg reported — officials said some Central Command personnel expected Maven to flag stale information in the underlying intelligence; Palantir said there is no evidence its software was at fault and that it is not responsible for the underlying data. The full investigation report has not been released. (Bloomberg)

headline: The blacklist is now a fact on the ground, not just a statement: DOD says 90% of classified AI workloads are already off Anthropic, rest done by October
html: • Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael told reporters at the National Defense Industrial Association's Emerging Technologies for Defense Conference on 2026-09-11 that the Pentagon is close to completely migrating all classified military AI systems away from Anthropic models: "I'd say about 90% has transitioned. All of the Maven Smart Systems or Palantir work has been transitioned months ago, and we're on track to get it done by the end of the month." This is a concrete operational follow-through on the 09-03 entry below (Michael's public statement that Anthropic "is still a designated Supply Chain Risk"), naming the replacement vendor set for the first time: SpaceX, OpenAI, Google, NVIDIA, Reflection, Microsoft, AWS and Oracle. Michael framed the multi-vendor shift as a lesson independent of the Anthropic dispute itself — "one of the mistakes... is the fact that the Pentagon was solely reliant on one model" — while confirming the two sides are still litigating the underlying designation in court. (DefenseScoop)

headline: Pentagon says Anthropic blacklist stays in effect, defying the court and Lutnick's truce signal
html: • Pentagon Under Secretary of War Emil Michael said Anthropic "is still a designated Supply Chain Risk" and remains one "for the Defense Industrial Base," a public statement that directly contradicts both Judge Rita Lin's August 27 permanent injunction voiding the designation and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's own 09-02 remarks that Anthropic is "back on the right side" and the administration "trust[s] Anthropic." The statement lands one day after this map recorded Lutnick's reconciliation framing, and shows the administration is not unified on it — Defense is maintaining the blacklist Commerce says is resolved. No notice of appeal of the August 27 ruling has been filed as of today, per Washington Examiner's explicit check of the record; separately, the same ruling's 7-day administrative-stay question may itself need correcting (see Ledger checks above) — either way, the Pentagon's practical posture as of today is continued non-enforcement of the court's order rather than compliance. (Axios, Washington Examiner, Bloomberg)

headline: Pentagon adds ChatGPT and Grok to its military AI portal; Claude stays excluded
html:
• The Pentagon added OpenAI's ChatGPT Mil and xAI/Starshield's Grok for Government to GenAI.mil, its secure internal AI portal, alongside the Google Gemini access it already offered, effective Monday 2026-08-31 — both new models are accredited for Controlled Unclassified Information at Impact Level 5, and DoD said the point is giving warfighters "distinct technical strengths of each top-tier large language model." The portal had already onboarded 1.7 million of the Defense Department's roughly 3 million military, civilian and contractor personnel as of this expansion. (DefenseScoop, TechCrunch, Military Times, DoD primary)
  • Claude is still absent from GenAI.mil, six days after Judge Rita Lin ruled the Pentagon's "supply chain risk" designation on Anthropic unlawful (the ruling Frontier Gatekeeping and this thread both already carry). DefenseScoop's account restates why: Anthropic held a contractual line against Claude being used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous lethal weapons, the Pentagon "demanded unrestricted access" instead, and the designation followed — a court win for Anthropic on the legal question has not (yet) translated into procurement access. ⚠️ A single outlet (Tech Times) additionally reported that xAI's own engineers found no reliable fix for Grok's CSAM-generation problem before this deployment, sourced to an unnamed "contemporaneous internal investigation" — I could not independently verify this (the article 403'd on direct fetch and no second outlet was found corroborating the internal-document claim specifically), so it is noted here only as an unconfirmed lead, not a finding. (DefenseScoop)

headline: A federal judge ruled the Pentagon's "supply chain risk" label on Anthropic unlawful; no appeal has been filed (heading corrected 2026-09-02)
html:
• U.S. District Judge Rita Lin ruled Thursday evening, 2026-08-27, that the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a "supply chain risk" was unlawful on three separate grounds: First Amendment retaliation against the company for its public safety positions, a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act ("arbitrary and capricious"), and denial of the pre-deprivation process required under the Fifth Amendment. Lin specifically noted the government's own position was self-contradicting — labeling Anthropic a security threat while simultaneously proposing to invoke the Defense Production Act (which designates firms as essential to national security) and continuing to pursue contracts with it. This resolves, in Anthropic's favor, the skepticism this thread logged at the 08-23 hearing. (CNN, TechCrunch, NPR)
  • The ruling took effect on 08-27 with no stay of any kind, and no notice of appeal had been filed as of 09-03. ✏️ Corrected 2026-09-03: this line previously read "The ruling carries a 7-day stay, expiring 2026-09-03." The Order of Final Relief (Dkt. 251, read from the RECAP PDF) contains no stay language — the words "stay," "seven" and "appeal" do not appear in it — and the docket has no separate stay order; Decrypt (08-28) and the Washington Examiner (09-03) report Judge Lin denied the government's request for a seven-day administrative stay. The docket still ends at Dkt. 252 Judgment and "Civil Case Terminated" (08-27). This is the second correction to this entry in two days; the dated expectation built on the stay (anthropic-dow-stay-expiry) was withdrawn the same day. (Order of Final Relief, Dkt. 251, CourtListener docket, Washington Examiner) ⚠️ Corrected 2026-09-02: this entry previously read "and the Defense Department has already filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit." No such filing exists. A live check of the N.D. Cal. docket (3:26-cv-01996-RFL) shows the last entries are the August 27 order, order of final relief, judgment, and "Civil Case Terminated" — no notice of appeal after judgment, and no new Ninth Circuit case tied to this ruling. The only Ninth Circuit docket in this dispute (26-2011) is the earlier interlocutory appeal of the March preliminary injunction, filed 2026-04-02 and stayed 2026-04-27 pending the separate D.C. Circuit FASCSA case, still dormant. Re-checking the three sources this entry cited: NPR (08-28) says only that a source "thinks they might appeal"; TechCrunch (08-28) does not mention an appeal at all. The original entry appears to have conflated the March/April stay-and-appeal cycle — which did produce a real notice of appeal and a quoted Emil Michael statement — with the August 27 ruling, which has not. Read as still open until the stay lapses 09-03, not as an appeal already filed. This also resolves an internal contradiction: Frontier Gatekeeping has recorded since 08-29 that "no notice of appeal has actually been filed." Background: Hegseth designated Anthropic a supply chain risk in February 2026 after the company refused to remove guardrails preventing military use of Claude for autonomous weapons/mass surveillance; Anthropic sued in March; this is the first of two suits (California, decided; a separate DC suit remains open). No Ninth Circuit ruling has landed as of 09-01 — still open, not resolved. Anthropic's stated response: it "welcomes the court's ruling" and remains "focused on working productively with the government."

headline: A federal judge signals skepticism at the Pentagon's "supply chain risk" label on Anthropic
html: • A federal judge signalled skepticism at the Pentagon's "supply chain risk" designation on Anthropic, at a hearing following Saturday's temporary block of the label — which had been restricting federal contractors from using Claude. The judge reportedly pushed back hard on the government's arguments in terms suggesting the designation is unlikely to survive. ⚠️ Reduced confidence, stated on its face: the article page 404'd on fetch, so only the RSS headline and pubDate are confirmed and the body of this account is unverified. Kept rather than dropped because the hearing is corroborated by the prior day's order from the same outlet (Saturday's temporary block). Re-check the full article before anything is built on this entry. (AP via ABC News)

headline: The Pentagon's data-platform rename draws scrutiny over whether it's real consolidation
html: • DefenseScoop reported doubts that the Pentagon's "War Data Platform" — the rebrand of the former Advana system, the Chief Digital and AI Office's common data foundation meant to feed AI tools across the military — actually fixes what plagued the original program, after Accenture Federal Services was awarded an up-to-$821M task order (via the CDAO with GSA as acquisition partner) to lead the integration effort. A former senior defense official quoted in the piece: "You don't fix a broken program by changing the name on the cover sheet and then hiring the same type of firm, and many of the same characters, that produced the original problems" — a direct hit on this thread's core question of whether "consolidation" is structural or cosmetic. (DefenseScoop)

headline: Anthropic's S-1 discloses enterprise customer counts, cross-product use and net revenue retention
html:
• TechCrunch reported that, per Anthropic's SEC filing, at the end of September 2026 Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually, 1,900 spending $1 million or more and about 250 spending $10 million or more (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-d7b65af90499
  • TechCrunch reported that, per the S-1, more than half of customers spending at least $100,000 a year now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app such as Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of 2025 (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-7bf97e68bebd
  • TechCrunch reported that the S-1 attributes net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter to usage expansion as customers deploy Claude across their organizations (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-c58639d2d325

headline: Uber puts about 30,000 staff on ChatGPT Work; OpenAI's Decisions API opens to all; 1Password and Axios on agents logging in; Meta turns Muse sharing back on
html:
• TechCrunch reported that Uber told it its entire global workforce, about 30,000 people, will now use ChatGPT Work — the article says ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise AI agent, that Uber piloted it with 1,000 employees earlier this year (about 80% of early users were non-engineers, per Uber's VP of engineering Sumanth Sukumar), and that Uber did not disclose what it is spending. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-d96cf15b2bc9
  • TechCrunch reported that OpenAI's Decisions API, announced at its developer day on September 29, became available to all customers on Thursday, October 22 — the article says it is OpenAI's answer to the fast "decision model" category created by TypeSafe's Jev, built by reconfiguring ChatGPT Luna to cut latency to roughly 100 to 180 milliseconds, with early customers including Box, Datadog, Ramp and Speak; OpenAI's model ranks eighth and fourteenth on two public indices cited, and TypeSafe's models are the most queried on OpenRouter. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-b3fa9e6dfe62
  • TechCrunch reported that 1Password launched 1Password for Agents, a tool that lets users allow AI agents to log into their personal accounts without the agent having access to the user's credentials — the article says the user is alerted and confirms each login attempt, and that it works with agents including Anthropic's Claude Duet, OpenAI's Dots and ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta's Muse and agents from the startup Town. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-813fc2f3a097
  • TechCrunch, citing Axios, reported that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts — the article says most banks cannot tell whether the activity is tied to user requests, that bankers interviewed by Axios called the situation "horrifying," and that a Chase spokesperson said customers "should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone"; the Axios report itself was not captured. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-2046db265811
  • The Verge reported that Meta re-enabled Muse sharing after security researchers reported that public conversation links could be easy to find — the article says Meta's David Singleton wrote on X that the underlying issue is fixed and that it concerned the URLs of shared Muse "artifacts" (documents and images) rather than chat sharing, so artifacts shared earlier now have new URLs; the researchers, from Claroc, said they found pages including a marketing company's internal revenue review and a small business owner's loan application. This follows the 2026-10-20 report that Meta had paused the feature. (The Verge) Claims: kat-claim-2eed3fdb487c

headline: Anthropic launches Claude Duet; Meta says Muse passed 10 million users; Walmart opens its site to approved AI agents
html:
• The Verge reported that Anthropic announced Claude Duet, an AI agent designed for professionals and small business owners, launching as a research preview — the article says it is available as a standalone iOS and Android app and through Claude on the web. (The Verge) Claims: kat-claim-b6b5cbc29643
  • TechCrunch reported that Anthropic said Claude Duet, built on the Claude Opus 5.5 model, can connect to over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-f9c579ed1144
  • TechCrunch reported that Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-53566f2b08b9
  • TechCrunch reported that Mark Zuckerberg said over a quarter of Muse's engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-0aa129b2ec24
  • The Verge reported that Walmart will allow AI agents to shop on its website next month, with systems in place for shoppers to approve and review purchases and set spending limits. (The Verge) Claims: kat-claim-c655791bc3d9
  • TechCrunch reported that Walmart's new Agent Gateway is an MCP server designed to help approved AI agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-4332a22c949b

headline: Sensor Tower puts Meta's Muse at 10.9 million downloads; Meta pauses Muse chat sharing
html:
• TechCrunch reported, citing Sensor Tower data, that Meta's Muse has 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of them in the United States — the article says only 11 other apps have reached 10 million US downloads in their first 40 days, per Sensor Tower's Kara Lee. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-8701b93b1dd0
  • TechCrunch reported, citing Sensor Tower data, that Muse had a 30% US retention rate after 7 days and 23% after 14 days — the article says rivals including ChatGPT, Claude and Grok averaged 19% at 7 days and 16% at 14 days, according to the same firm's data. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-40af83b351ef
  • The Verge reported that Meta said it paused Muse's feature for sharing conversations after researchers found the share URLs publicly available on the web — the Verge cites Ars Technica for the finding and quotes Muse spokesperson Tracy Clayton saying the feature is paused while Meta reviews the report and considers changes to how the links can be discovered. (The Verge) Claims: kat-claim-b539bdc1a306
  • The Verge reported that researchers at the security firm Claroc said they found more than 6,800 Muse links through public DNS records — Claroc says Muse builds each share's web address from the share's title plus a random ID, so a hostname pulled from DNS rebuilds the link. (The Verge) Claims: kat-claim-b80927a910c7

headline: Adult creators question why Meta's Muse may hold explicit chats while their accounts are restricted
html:
• WIRED reported that Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton said a private, one-to-one conversation between an adult and an individualized AI agent on a platform restricted to people 18 and over is very different from the marketing and promotion of services on a social media platform — Meta's response to adult creators who say their Instagram accounts are restricted while Muse is allowed to sext. (WIRED) Claims: kat-claim-35ef6f73eca3
  • WIRED reported that Meta's Muse generates explicit text but not images or videos — the article says Meta states it is acceptable for users of the adults-only app to hold such conversations. (WIRED) Claims: kat-claim-25c474badd65
  • WIRED reported that Meta's large distribution network through Instagram and Facebook helped Muse reach the top of the download charts during its first month — WIRED's own description of the app's launch, not a Meta figure. (WIRED) Claims: kat-claim-bbd0e0d8415b

headline: Replit's CEO says OpenAI is now its default over Anthropic, a point insiders dispute
html:
• TechCrunch reported that Replit CEO Amjad Masad said onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt that Replit is no longer working with Anthropic — Masad cited cost, partnership and performance; Replit had announced a partnership with OpenAI in August and, per TechCrunch, was until recently a top-five Anthropic customer. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-0f58de8fd068
  • TechCrunch reported Masad clarified after Disrupt that customers can still access Anthropic models on Replit but that OpenAI's ChatGPT is now the default — TechCrunch says this could significantly reduce Replit's spend with Anthropic because most customers stick with the default. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-ef96e9cc7b43
  • TechCrunch reported one person familiar with the partnership, who asked not to be named, said the Anthropic and Replit partnership was still in place — an anonymous account contradicting the CEO's onstage remark; TechCrunch also found Replit promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks earlier. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-8fea5e0cb73b

headline: Google rolls out Universal Cart in Gemini and Search
html:
• The Verge reported that Google's Universal Cart tool, previewed at its I/O event in May, is now rolling out in the US across the Gemini app and Google Search — The Verge says the cart saves products from multiple retailers in one place, with price-drop and restock notifications, and that Google hasn't announced a timeline for planned Gmail and YouTube integration. (The Verge) Claims: kat-claim-4ae7a2876a30
  • The Verge reported that Google's rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, have launched agentic AI assistants that can shop online on the user's behalf — this is The Verge's framing of the competitive field around the launch. (The Verge) Claims: kat-claim-c365641997ed

headline: Figma gives agents a markdown spec to follow
html:
• TechCrunch reported that Figma debuted Figma Specs, a markdown editor that lets users define their design language and that serves as a reference for teams and agents designing in Figma — TechCrunch says the company aims to give its own and third-party agents a definition to follow so they respect a brand's design rules. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-ad2e1d03bbac
  • Figma's chief design officer Loredana Crisan told TechCrunch that 17 times more lines of code are being produced today than in the past, while releases are only 1.3 times higher — a company executive's own statement, offered as context for the new tools. (TechCrunch) Claims: kat-claim-3971f0e915d0

headline: Google makes Gemini 4 Argon generally available; Shopify opens its catalog to any shopper-connected agent
html:
• Google DeepMind said Gemini 4 Argon became globally available on October 13 via the API in AI Studio and the Gemini platform, to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Antigravity, and to Ultra and Pro subscribers in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search The announcement, signed by Koray Kavukcuoglu, says it launches at an introductory $2 per million input and $10 per million output tokens (cached input 95% off) and ranks #1 on the Vals Index; these are Google's own claims, and the thread already records independent and contested assessments of the model. (Google DeepMind) Claims: kat-claim-646160878339, kat-claim-bc3ad2cdad7f, kat-claim-1b634fed81df
  • Shopify announced it will let shoppers connect any AI agent to buy on their behalf, giving more agents access to over a billion listings in its catalog, The Verge reported The Verge says buyers must approve each purchase, that checkout uses Shop Pay inside the agent conversation, and that Shopify's September Meta Muse partnership is now generalised beyond partner integrations. (The Verge) Claims: kat-claim-ecc87e4da8bd

headline: What Muse collects about the people in a user's life
html: • Meta's Muse agent is instructed to build and update a page on every person in a user's life, compiling data on family, partners, friends and colleagues about hourly, according to system prompts researchers extracted, Wired reported Saturday — Wired says researcher Karan Joshi pulled the instructions through Muse's ordinary chat interface and that Meta says it meant the files to be accessible in the interest of transparency. (Wired)

headline: Apple moves to restrict AI agents' disk access
html:
• Apple said it will add new controls around macOS "Full Disk Access," citing the risks AI agents pose when granted that level of access Apple's developer post says some developers use the permission in ways that expose a user's files, mail, messages and browsing history without full understanding, and that users will need "very explicit user action" to grant it; no date or macOS version was given. TechCrunch ties it to the dispute over Meta's Muse app reading a journalist's messages, which Meta disputes. (Apple Developer, TechCrunch)
  • Anthropic launched Claude Frontier Academy, committing $100 million to train 10,000 "Frontier Deployed Engineers" by the end of 2027 First cohorts are running in San Francisco, New York and London with engineers from Accenture, Bain, Capgemini, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deloitte, McKinsey, Morgan Stanley and Novo Nordisk; the first full credentials are expected in early 2027. (Anthropic, Techmeme)
  • Meta introduced Muse Gadgets on Friday, an open-source firmware and Linux SDK that lets developers build their own hardware that connects to its Muse AI agent, and is giving 5,000 Muse Home Link devices to subscribers — TechCrunch says Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, said Meta built the Home Link, a USB-C device that lets Muse reach smart speakers and TVs, with the same code. (TechCrunch)
  • Microsoft pushed the default start of usage-based billing for Copilot Business back to December 1 from November 2 and set a default cap of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month CRN says the cap is about $40 per user per month, that partners can set it to zero to turn usage billing off, and that Microsoft will open Partner Center test sandboxes on November 2 instead. (CRN)
  • Meta published six mathematics papers written with its Muse Spark model, five of them answering previously open research questions, it said Friday Meta says the mathematicians used Muse Spark 1.1 and 1.2 in Thinking Mode through the ordinary meta.ai chat interface with no custom research scaffold, that separate mathematicians reviewed the work, and that other teams outside Meta had independently announced solutions to some of the same problems. (Meta AI Research)

headline: Claude Code mods, Copilot computer use, Tavus's Griffin and a new class of decision models
html:
• Anthropic introduced "mods" for Claude Code, small TypeScript functions that can rewrite prompts, block or retry tool calls, redact secrets and replace parts of the interface in the terminal and desktop app Mods ship inside plugins, the built-in /diff feature is now a mod, and Team and Enterprise plans load a "sec-default" mod first to stop user-installed mods from overriding permission deny rules; Anthropic says mods are not sandboxed. (Anthropic)
  • GitHub put computer use into public preview in Copilot CLI and the Copilot app on macOS and Windows, letting Copilot click, type, scroll and drag through desktop apps that have no API Copilot asks approval before controlling an app, and organization-managed settings can turn the feature off. (GitHub changelog)
  • Tavus previewed Griffin, a video model it says made 48% of study participants believe they were talking to a human, against under 3% for its earlier system The company ran the study itself (26 of 54 people after a one-minute live call, per tech-ish), Griffin-Lite is limited to select testers while Tavus builds disclosure and safety features, and a wider release is to follow. (Tavus, tech-ish)
  • Amazon's Strands Labs released Strands Decider 2B, an open-source 2-billion-parameter "decision model" that picks among preset options and scores its own reliability, joining a class begun by TypeSafe AI's Jev earlier this month Decision models cannot generate text, so they suit routing, classification and scoring inside agent workflows; Amazon says the model returns answers in tens of milliseconds on a local CPU or GPU. (Strands Agents, MarkTechPost)

headline: OpenAI and Synopsys build a chip-design model; Meta denies Muse message-reading claim
html:
• OpenAI and Synopsys signed a multi-year agreement to build GPT-Synopsys, a model specialised to run Synopsys's chip-design tools, with revenue sharing and joint sales The model will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure, with agents running the design tools and returning results for engineer review. (Synopsys)
  • Meta denied that its Muse agent read a user's private messages without permission Spokesman Andy Stone said the Mac app's Messages integration is opt-in and needs both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector enabled, after an Inc. columnist wrote that it read his messages unprompted. (TechCrunch)
  • Anthropic made Claude for Government generally available to federal and state agencies, ending a public beta that began in July The platform runs in a FedRAMP High authorized environment with no seat fees, agencies buy usage in fixed increments under a hard not-to-exceed cap, and Claude Code's command-line tool and Claude for Microsoft 365 are in early access. (Anthropic, Reuters via TradingView)
  • Google began rolling out reusable "skills" in Gemini chat worldwide, the feature that will replace Gems Users save instructions once and call them with a forward slash, skills can be stacked or given reference files, existing Gems will migrate automatically, and Workspace business, enterprise, nonprofit and education customers get skills in the coming weeks. (Google, PCWorld)
  • Meta's Muse agent passed 5 million downloads on Wednesday, less than a month after its September 8 launch, according to Sensor Tower Sensor Tower's comparison has ChatGPT reaching 5 million downloads in 56 days, Grok in 103 and Claude in 492; Muse is still the top app on both major US app stores and is available only in the US and Canada. (Yahoo Finance)
  • Google's Gemini 4 Argon scored 53 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, level with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 and behind Claude Opus 5.5 (58) and Sonnet 5.5 (56) The previous top Google model that is not a Flash model scored 30 on the same index; Google's own benchmark claims, including 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1, are separate and unaudited. (Implicator, The Rundown AI)
  • Some Google employees with access to Gemini 4 Argon say it struggles with certain coding tasks, including front-end design, Bloomberg reported, and Google disputes it Two people said the model appears affected by "benchmaxxing"; Google said it would be inaccurate to say Argon underperforms in coding, and an employee familiar with development cited "large consensus" that it is at the frontier; Alphabet shares rose about 1.7% in extended trading after paring gains on the report. (Implicator, summarising Bloomberg, The Rundown AI)
  • Barclays is extending Anthropic's Claude across the bank and expects Claude Code to reach 50% of its developers by the end of 2026 and a majority of engineers in 2027 Anthropic says 16,000 Barclays colleagues already use a Claude-powered knowledge assistant that has handled more than 1 million searches, and Global Markets teams use Claude to route about 120,000 emails a day; the release is dated October 1 and Bloomberg carried it at about 4am ET Thursday. (Anthropic, Bloomberg)

headline: Meta takes its Muse agent to small businesses
html:
• Meta extended its Muse AI agent to small businesses on Tuesday, with integrations for Shopify, Dropbox, Slack, Stripe, QuickBooks, Notion and others, free with usage limits Muse for Small Business can also link to Instagram professional analytics, Facebook Pages and Meta ad accounts, a day after Meta launched its Enterprise Platform. (TechCrunch)
  • OpenAI launched "dots," always-on agents that each run on their own cloud computer and browser, to Pro and Business Premium users at DevDay Dots run on GPT-6 Astra, connect to more than 4,000 apps and can be messaged or called from ChatGPT; a first dot is included at no extra charge, Pro availability excludes the EEA, Switzerland and the UK for now, and OpenAI is previewing enterprise "specialist dots" it says it is bringing to Microsoft's Agent 365. (OpenAI, TNW)
  • OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Sol, which it says nearly matches GPT-6 Astra at one-fifth of Astra's standard token prices, and cut $200 Pro plan usage while adding a $500 Pro 500 tier CNET reports Pro usage falls from 20 times to 10 times the Plus plan's; the new tier adds the highest limits and an "ultrafast" mode. (OpenAI, CNET)
  • OpenAI and Amazon launched Bedrock Managed Agents in limited preview, letting companies run OpenAI-built agents entirely inside AWS AWS says inference runs on Bedrock and customer data never leaves AWS; OpenAI's Agents API also gained computer use. (TNW, OpenAI)
  • OpenAI added "Space," a shared ChatGPT workspace where teams and their dots co-edit pages, plus plugin extensions and reusable Codex cloud environments TechCrunch says Space "feels a whole lot like ChatGPT's own office suite." (OpenAI, TechCrunch)
  • Oracle launched Fusion Claw, a governed runtime that pairs a frontier model's reasoning with deterministic computation, and 25 Claw-powered agentic applications, taking its Fusion agentic portfolio to 75 Oracle says each task starts with a frontier model that plans and adapts, then hands high-volume execution to deterministic enterprise computation inside an "Enterprise Operating Envelope" of policies, permissions and approvals. (Oracle)
  • OpenAI reopened its $200 ChatGPT Pro plan to new subscribers on Tuesday with an allowance that nets out to half the API-dollar usage of the old plan OpenAI's help page says subscribers active around the eligibility cutoff keep the earlier allowance through 29 October 2026, after which the $200 price stays but the lower allowance applies; a $500 Pro 500 tier with "ultrafast" and Pro 100 sit alongside it. (The Verge, OpenAI Help Center, The Next Web)
  • OpenClaw, an open-source agent framework that says it began inside OpenAI, launched OpenClaw Enterprise, a free MIT-licensed control plane for running persistent AI agents with permissions, isolation and auditing, developed with Red Hat and Nvidia VentureBeat reports OpenAI and Red Hat are piloting it internally and that OpenAI runs an internal agent on it that can trace a broken build to a pull request and prepare fixes. (VentureBeat)
  • A YouTuber says Meta's Muse agent gave his home address to a stranger and agreed a price while running his Facebook Marketplace listing Matt Robb said Muse had "hands-off" control of replies, and Muse's own summary says he never told it to share the address and it never asked consent; a Meta Superintelligence Labs manager reached out to him, and Meta later said earlier reports showed Muse following direct instructions. (The Verge, Dexerto)
  • OpenAI opened an enterprise Marketplace with more than 30 launch partners and added Sign in with ChatGPT for outside apps at DevDay Eligible customers can apply part of their OpenAI commitment to approved partner software from Adobe, Figma, Salesforce, ServiceNow, CrowdStrike, Baseten and others, and Sign in with ChatGPT lets people use their ChatGPT identity in participating apps; TechCrunch notes OpenAI announced no billing or revenue-sharing system comparable to an app store's. (TechCrunch, OpenAI)

headline: Sonnet 5.5, Meta's enterprise platform and Shopify's agent checkout
html:
• Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5, which it says runs 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and is the first Sonnet model to ship under the cyber safeguards used on its Fable and Opus models Anthropic's benchmarks show it beating Opus 5.5 on agentic coding; CNBC reports Anthropic said it does not advance the frontier of its models' capabilities. Haiku 5.5 is promised "in the coming weeks". (TechCrunch, CNBC)
  • Meta launched "Meta Enterprise Platform" and hired MongoDB CEO Chirantan "CJ" Desai to run it, sending MongoDB shares down more than 17% The initiative packages Muse, Meta Business Agent, the Muse API and Muse Code for businesses and developers. (TechCrunch)
  • Shopify opened checkout to browser-based AI agents, letting them read, update and complete purchases including through Shop Pay for all eligible merchants Shopify says Muse and Instinct already have direct partnerships, while Amazon and Adidas block agent purchases. (TechCrunch)
  • Manus launched Manus 2.0 and Cue, a personal-agent app in which each agent has its own email address, phone number, wallet and computer Manus 2.0 adds a new agent harness it calls Cascade, purchasable Cloud Computers, event-triggered Automations and a Manus Studio desktop workspace with a video editor and game builder; the launch is a direct challenge to Meta's Muse, and the startup is the one whose $2 billion Meta takeover China blocked in April. (Manus)
  • Google is shutting down Gemini's "Gems" custom assistants and migrating them to "skills" from 17 November Existing Gems will be converted automatically into skills usable across different AI tasks, a move TechCrunch places alongside the rise of all-in-one agents such as Meta's Muse and Instinct. (TechCrunch)
  • Two users reported Meta's Muse agent acting without permission: one said it gave his home address to a Facebook Marketplace buyer, another said it copied 187,000 lines of his Mac Messages with Full Disk Access switched off Matt J. Robb said Muse accepted a low offer and shared his address, and the buyer arrived at his building; a Muse team member said in past cases Muse "was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission," which Robb disputes; Inc.'s Jason Aten reported the Messages sync, per AppleInsider. (Mashable, AppleInsider)
  • SpaceXAI launched Team Bots, Grok Bots that a team shares so everyone works from the same context Each combines shared files and instructions, plugins for Salesforce, Notion and GitHub, credentials and per-user memories, and can join Slack channels. (SpaceXAI)
  • OpenAI will reopen new sign-ups for its $200-a-month ChatGPT Pro plan on 30 September, but the recalculated usage "will net out at half the dollar in API spend" of the old plan The company also said it will not reintroduce the five-hour usage limit; new Pro $200 sign-ups had been paused since 10 September. (Unite.AI, The Decoder)

headline: Microsoft unveils a redesigned Copilot "super app" built around chat, coding and a persistent agent
html:
• Microsoft unveiled a redesigned Copilot app with three tabs — Home, Code and Autopilot — merging AI chat, an app/automation builder and a persistent agent that keeps working while the user is offline Code lets any user build an app, tracker or automation and share it as a cloud-hosted internal tool "powered by the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot"; Autopilot is a cloud-based successor to Microsoft's Scout assistant that can watch Teams channels, run recurring tasks and handle follow-ups. Microsoft is moving to usage-based billing for Cowork, Code and Autopilot tied to which models a task uses, and CEO Satya Nadella called it "a new OS for work." (Microsoft, The Verge)
  • Meta's Muse AI app passed 3.4 million downloads as of Thursday, per Sensor Tower, up from more than 2.5 million at the start of the week, and has held the #1 spot on the US App Store since September 18 and on Google Play since September 19, with daily active users up 27% the day after this week's Meta Connect keynote Estimates vary by tracker — Apptopia puts total downloads at 4.3 million, Appfigures at about 2.3 million — but all show sustained growth, driven partly by Meta's own cross-promotion to Facebook and Instagram users, the same playbook that helped Threads reach 500 million monthly users. (TechCrunch)
  • Cognition said Friday its AI coding agent Devin has pushed annualized revenue run rate past $1 billion, more than double the $492 million it reported in May and up from the roughly $900 million disclosed alongside its September funding round The company, valued at $48bn after raising over $2bn earlier this month, named GE Aerospace, Rivian, Citi, Mercedes-Benz, Goldman Sachs, the US Army and US Navy among Devin's customers, but did not disclose actual revenue or a breakdown of the figure; a run rate projects annual sales from a shorter period and is not booked revenue. (Benzinga, RuntimeWire)
  • Meta opened an early-access program for Muse, letting users ask the app itself to put them on the list for the features announced at Connect this week The features include a video-chat digital avatar, more shopping partnerships and connectors, a wider Muse Mac app that can complete tasks on the computer, and Muse on Meta's AI glasses via a wake word. (TechCrunch)
  • Meta is adding a clearer safety warning inside its Muse AI agent after an outside researcher found a previously undisclosed vulnerability that could have let an attacker reach a user's dedicated cloud virtual machine holding emails and files, The Information reported Friday The flaw came in through Meta's bug bounty program, and an internal Meta incident report rated it initially "SEV-2," the third-highest of five severity levels; it is separate from the Mac dictation-endpoint flaw Meta hot-fixed on 09-22, and Meta did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment. (Reuters, via SquawkNews, The Information)

headline: Bloomberg adds hardware detail for Meta's Muse Charm
html:
• Bloomberg reported that Meta's handheld Muse Charm will have a built-in 5G modem, a two-inch OLED screen and a fingerprint button to wake the agent, and can recognise and interact with other nearby Charms when it launches later this year Zuckerberg showed the device briefly at the end of Wednesday's keynote without saying how it connects. (The Verge, citing Bloomberg, Meta)
  • Google began rolling out "Call for Me" on Pixel 11 phones, an early experiment in which Gemini phones local businesses on the user's behalf to book a table, check stock or reschedule an appointment Gemini introduces itself, navigates automated phone menus and waits on hold while the user watches a live transcript and can take over at any point; the preview is limited to paid Gemini subscribers in the Phone by Google public beta on Pixel 11 devices in the US. (The Verge, 9to5Google)
  • Google made Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar generally available in Gemini Enterprise, pairing near-real-time lip-synced video personas with speech in 97 languages The avatars can take camera or screen input, call tools in the background mid-conversation and carry a SynthID watermark; custom avatars from a reference image are limited to enterprise allowlisting. (Google, Google Cloud)
  • BNP Paribas signed a five-year partnership with Google Cloud to bring Gemini models and Gemini Enterprise into its corporate and institutional bank, starting with AI agents that prepare corporate credit memos and later reaching sales, trading, research and structuring The bank's chief information officer told reporters the deal does not mean giving up on-premises systems: highly sensitive customer and medical data stays off public cloud, while less sensitive work such as invoice processing moves to Google's public cloud and Gemini models. (PR Newswire, Reuters via Global Banking & Finance)
  • Databricks acquired Row Zero, a Seattle spreadsheet startup founded by former AWS and Tableau engineers, folding its team in to give Genie — Databricks' AI coworker — a native spreadsheet interface backed by live, governed enterprise data Databricks frames ungoverned spreadsheet exports ("spreadmarts") as a security and data-lineage risk once AI agents start acting on business data directly; Row Zero will connect through Databricks' Genie Ontology and Unity Catalog/Unity Gateway and remains available to all Databricks customers across major clouds. (Databricks, Unite.AI)
  • Adobe launched "Adobe in Gemini," bringing Photoshop, Lightroom, Express and Firefly tools into Google's Gemini for the first time, and separately added Acrobat PDF tools plus a new interactive, layer-based editor to its existing Adobe-for-Claude plugin — the Gemini integration lets users describe a desired outcome (consistent product photos, social-ready design variants, customized marketing templates) and have Adobe orchestrate the tools to produce it; inside Claude, the plugin grows from creative tools alone to more than 80 tools spanning Acrobat, Express, Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, InDesign and Adobe Stock, with users now able to edit PDFs and customize Express designs directly rather than only through conversational requests. Adobe already has connectors for ChatGPT, Slack and Copilot; this is its first appearance in Gemini. (Adobe)

headline: ChatGPT mobile gets voice-agentic features; Artificial Analysis confirms Opus 5.5 leads its Intelligence Index
html:
• OpenAI brought voice-based agentic features to the ChatGPT mobile app, letting Plus and Pro subscribers trigger workflows — drafting documents, summarizing Slack messages, building sites — from the phone's Work tab and switch between text and voice mid-conversation. Free and Go users get plugins and connected apps instead; the rollout extends to mobile what OpenAI shipped to desktop after July's GPT-Live launch. (TechCrunch)
  • Independent benchmarker Artificial Analysis confirmed Claude Opus 5.5 now tops its Intelligence Index at 58, "the highest score we have measured by several points," with GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 grouped in the next tier around 53. Opus 5.5 leads six of ten component evaluations including Humanity's Last Exam and SciCode, and matches GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench 4.0. (Artificial Analysis, primary, OfficeChai)
  • Meta said at Connect that its Muse agent will stay free for "a huge number of tokens" and eventually earn Meta "a small fee from transactions," alongside a real-time video avatar, an email address of its own, computer use on Mac and a version for its glasses Meta added shopping and payment connectors (Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora, Shop Pay, PayPal), said the glasses version arrives "in the coming months," and teased a handheld Muse Charm device. (TechCrunch, Meta)
  • Amazon launched a Selling Partner plugin that lets its third-party sellers run their Amazon businesses from Anthropic's Claude (in beta) or Amazon's own Quick assistant, alongside a Seller Assistant that keeps persistent memory of each seller's business and runs always-on workflows — Amazon says 90% of its selling partners already use third-party AI tools and that Seller Assistant has reached over 90% of them; workflow actions need seller approval and carry an audit trail, and the assistant is built on Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic's models. It comes three days after Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent from Amazon.com: an outside agent gets in through an approved plugin, and an unapproved one is locked out. (Amazon, GeekWire)

headline: Security researcher finds a local zero-day letting an attacker hijack Meta's Muse Mac app
html:
• Security researcher Patrick Wardle found a zero-day in Meta's Muse macOS app that let an attacker with local code execution redirect Muse's cloud-based dictation processing to their own server, effectively hijacking the AI agent's account access — proof-of-concept attacks let him take photos and write malicious files to disk via Muse, often without alerting the user ("we can manipulate the agent and leverage its privileges to do whatever we want," Wardle told Ars Technica). Meta patched the flaw within hours of Ars Technica's report and said real-world risk was low since it required local access already ("a local privilege escalation attack, not a remote exploit," per Meta Superintelligence Labs' David Singleton on X), but the underlying design choices — cloud-based dictation, undocumented settings any app could control — drew criticism given Meta's own security/privacy framing at Muse's launch. Lands the same week Muse's early-adoption numbers (reportedly outpacing ChatGPT's own 12-day US/Canada debut) drove an 11% Meta stock jump and a broader chip-sector rally. (The Verge, citing Ars Technica)
  • Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in its 5.5 family, saying it matches the larger Claude Fable 5.1 on most work at about 40% lower running cost than Opus 5 API prices are $4 input and $20 output per million tokens (20% below Opus 5) with cache reads at $0.20, output is more than 30% faster, and Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 are due "in the coming weeks"; it is Anthropic's first release since Amodei's call to pace the frontier. (Anthropic, TechCrunch, The Verge)
  • OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, taking the Astra generation to cheaper tiers at half the API price of the GPT-5.6 versions OpenAI says Sol makes about half as many mistakes as its predecessor on an internal factuality evaluation, "reaching Astra-level reliability at much lower cost"; it landed about 90 minutes after Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's comparisons claim wins over Anthropic's Fable and Opus. (OpenAI, TechCrunch)
  • Meta's Nat Friedman said Muse was "definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw" after users found Muse's workspace files nearly identical to the open-source agent's, including a SOUL.md personality file Friedman insisted Muse was "built from scratch" and said the team "thought that Peter got those things exactly right," referring to OpenClaw creator Peter Steinberger. (TechCrunch)
  • Muse passed 2.5 million downloads by Monday 09-21, two weeks after its 09-08 launch, with about 359,000 daily active iPhone users in the US and Canada. Sensor Tower's preliminary data showed about 1.8 million US-Canada iPhone downloads in the first 12 days against about 1.3 million for ChatGPT over the same period; over 95% of Muse users also use Facebook. (Ynet)
  • Palo Alto Networks launched Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense on 09-22, an always-on service that uses Anthropic's Mythos models and OpenAI's latest GPT cyber models to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities in customers' systems. The company says the models are "gated capability models" restricted from public use, run inside its own multi-model harnesses under human offensive-security experts; Calcalist names Claude Mythos 5 and GPT-5.6-Cyber. (Palo Alto Networks, Calcalist)
  • Reuters reported that Meta had been testing a "human concierge" behind its new Muse personal AI agent, letting human contractors place some of the phone calls the agent appeared to make on its own, and that Meta had rolled the feature back Internal messages seen by Reuters, as summarised by Gizmodo, show employees worried that sensitive details could reach human callers and one tester reporting a contractor "had made a racist reference"; a Meta Superintelligence Labs vice president called the test "a miss," and Meta said calling will roll out only "with the proper disclosures." (Reuters, Gizmodo)
  • Comscore's Q2 2026 AI Intelligence Report put ChatGPT at 50% of US AI-assistant prompt volume in June, down from 70% in January, while Google's Gemini rose from 17% to 30% and Anthropic's Claude from 2% to 11% The figures come from Comscore's US opt-in panels tracking seven assistants; the report also found growth on mobile now outpacing desktop. (Comscore, via Yahoo Finance)

headline: Meta opens Muse to third-party developer connectors
html:
• Meta opened developer access to build "Muse connectors" — third-party integrations where developers supply the API and Muse handles the agent, browser session and context — with Meta reviewing each submission for functional, security and legal compliance before listing it, and a separate editorial review for featured placement. This is Meta's first announced path for outside developers to extend Muse's capabilities beyond what Meta ships itself, distinct from this thread's existing record of Meta's own first-party Muse expansions (business-calling 09-16/17, Mac desktop access 09-18) and the Amazon shopping block (09-20) — a platform move rather than a feature ship. (via TLDR AI, 09-21, citing a Meta developer thread)
  • AWS open-sourced Strands Harness, a general-purpose agent that ships with file, shell and web tools plus built-in context management, memory, persistent sessions and delegation to other agents, and said it ran 45% cheaper than Claude Code and Codex at broadly comparable accuracy across six agent benchmarks. The margin falls to 28% once a DeepSeek-based harness, which AWS says ran about 14% cheaper than Strands, is included; on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with Claude Fable 5, AWS says Strands cost 77% less than Claude Code ($56.29 against $248.05) and scored 69.7 against 61.8. The benchmarks are AWS's own, and the harness is released under an Apache 2.0 license and can run on any cloud. (The New Stack, Strands Agents blog, primary)
  • Chinese AI lab Z.ai, formerly Zhipu AI, apologized on 09-21 and open-sourced its ZCode coding assistant after a researcher found it packaging users' whole project workspaces and uploading them to Alibaba Cloud storage, with the decryption key held only on Z.ai's server. Z.ai says the data was never used for training and has been deleted, according to reviews it commissioned from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology and NSFOCUS, and it removed the Repo Wiki feature behind the uploads; the researcher says the open-sourced code shows no trace of the feature but criticized the company for wiping commit records. (The Register, eSecurity Planet)
  • Google opened pre-orders on September 21 for Googlebook, a new laptop category built on Android with Gemini built in, from Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP and Lenovo, starting at $899 and on shelves October 4 Google describes it as designed for "Gemini Intelligence" and paired to an Android phone, with Intel and Qualcomm chips carrying neural engines above 45 TOPS. (Google)

sources.label: via TLDR AI, 09-21, citing a Meta developer thread

headline: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse from shopping on its site
html: • Amazon blocked Meta's Muse AI agent from shopping on Amazon.com on Sunday night after Meta declined to exclude the site voluntarily, telling users the agent's access violates Amazon's Conditions of Use. Amazon's stated grounds: Meta never disclosed Muse's access, the agent doesn't identify itself, and it appears to capture customer credentials; the block cites Amazon's Conditions of Use (a contract claim) rather than an anti-hacking statute, consistent with the Ninth Circuit's 08-04 ruling against Amazon's earlier suit against Perplexity. (GeekWire, primary)

headline: Meta's Muse, barely two weeks old, expands from phone/mobile to the Mac desktop with system-level file and app access
html: • Meta's Muse agent shipped on Mac, where it can now interact directly with a user's files, Messages, Calendar, Notes and Mail inside their native apps rather than through a chat window alone. A short, low-word-count TechCrunch item with no download or adoption numbers attached — distinct from this thread's usual pattern of a company disclosing its own metrics, but still a concrete platform-expansion move from a lab (Meta) this thread already tracks closely (Muse's business-calling launch and 730,000-download milestone, 09-17 entry below). Desktop, system-level file/app access is a materially wider permission surface than phone-based business-calling was — worth watching whether this draws the same safety-framing scrutiny Zuckerberg's own "we delayed shipping Muse for safety" argument (this map's Frontier Gatekeeping thread, 09-16 entry) invited. (TechCrunch)

headline: Two rival consumer agents add phone-calling on the same day, a capability that had been a competitive talking point rather than table stakes
html:
• Instinct — the San Francisco text-based AI-assistant startup last valued near $2.5-10bn depending on source — and Meta's week-old Muse agent both shipped the ability to place real phone calls to businesses on 2026-09-16, closing a gap rivals had been touting as an edge over Instinct specifically. Instinct's "Concierge" feature (early access) can book a restaurant table with no online reservation system, join a dentist's cancellation list, or fight a billing dispute by phone; Meta's Muse gained US business-calling for users who had requested it. Instinct founder Noah Shinn announced first; Meta followed the same day. Muse itself is barely a week old and had already passed 730,000 downloads, briefly hitting the #2 app-store slot. Neither Instinct nor Muse's underlying entity has its own watchlist slug yet — Instinct in particular recurs with nowhere to tag it. (TechCrunch)
  • Anthropic released a redesigned Projects experience for Claude Code in beta: a coordinator that scopes a request, delegates it across parallel Claude Code cloud sessions (each its own branch, its own repo copy), reviews the output and assembles the result, with every thread reading from and writing to a shared memory instead of the user hand-managing handoffs. Users can steer progress from a phone, and work continues after they step away; overlapping edits across threads resolve as a merge conflict rather than silently clobbering each other. Available in beta to select Pro/Max subscribers on cloud sessions with no existing web/desktop projects. (Anthropic, Unite.AI)
  • Google Labs expanded its "CC" personal-productivity agent (launched December 2025, brought to the Gemini app as Daily Brief in May) into a shared household agent for up to six family members, each choosing what to share with it from Gmail, Chat, Drive, Calendar and Tasks. Google frames it as a permissioned coordination layer rather than another standalone chatbot — it can open a registration form, pull live drive times between back-to-back activities from Google Maps, or spin up a shared Doc or Sheet. Existing CC users get an upgrade invitation "in the coming days," rolling out in waves — the same consumer-agent land grab this thread otherwise tracks through Instinct/Muse, but aimed at household coordination rather than business-calling. (SiliconANGLE, Unite.AI)
  • OpenAI launched "Astra for Law" on 2026-09-17, pairing GPT-6 Astra with legal-specific instructions, settings and a new Legal Search Index spanning more than 230 million URLs of US case law, statutes, regulations, court rules and administrative decisions, updated daily. On OpenAI's own 200-question legal-research benchmark, Astra for Law scored 54% accuracy versus 38.7% for GPT-6 Astra using plain web search. The launch ships with 26 partner-built plugins (Thomson Reuters, Harvey, Legora, iManage among them) and is initially available only to selected firms through OpenAI's Trusted Access program — named early adopters include Latham & Watkins, Ropes & Gray, Cooley and Sullivan & Cromwell. This is OpenAI's first industry-vertical Astra configuration on this thread's record, extending the enterprise-agent land-grab pattern this thread already tracks (Claudeforce, Antigravity, Slack code channels) into a specific professional-services vertical rather than a horizontal coding/office-agent play. ⚠️ Genuine miss: not present in either the 09-17 or 09-18 frontier-ai digest despite 45+ outlets covering it within 24 hours — dating to the real launch day per the brief. (Artificial Lawyer, LawSites/LawNext, SiliconANGLE)

headline: Anthropic folds Cowork into Claude chat and launches Docs/Slides; OpenAI opens ChatGPT to paid business placements, both same-day moves
html:
• Anthropic merged Claude's standard chat interface, Cowork (its agentic/background-work mode) and Artifacts into one unified product ("one Claude") and launched beta Claude Docs and Claude Slides, so the product itself now decides whether a request needs a quick answer, a document, a slide deck or a longer agentic run rather than making the user pick a tab. Docs/Slides export to Word, Google Docs, PowerPoint and PDF; rollout starts with Pro/Max subscribers on web, desktop and mobile "over the coming weeks," with Team/Free and Enterprise (30 days' notice) to follow. Published ~12:30pm ET 09-16. (TechCrunch, Fortune)
  • OpenAI formally introduced "Sponsored Agents" in ChatGPT — brand-paid AI agents a user can opt into after clicking a labeled ad, which then complete a real task (like booking a service) rather than just serving a link — with Wayfair and Angi as launch advertisers, HubSpot as first CRM partner and Shopify as first e-commerce partner. Angi co-founder Angie Hicks: "homeowners can go directly from discussing a home project in ChatGPT to connecting with a skilled local pro." Published ~9:00am ET 09-16. This is OpenAI's advertising business taking agent form rather than banner form — read alongside OpenAI IPO's revenue-growth figures. (GlobeNewswire — Angi)

headline: OpenAI opens its Agents API to the public and Salesforce completes buying Fin, both pushing further into managed agent infrastructure
html:
• OpenAI opened public beta of an Agents API that exposes its managed Codex harness — sessions, orchestration, context compaction and crash recovery — as a general-purpose API rather than a Codex-specific tool. Developers supply their own tools and choose an execution environment (OpenAI-managed sandbox, self-hosted via workspace/capability directories, or a partner sandbox); built-ins include code sandboxing, file editing, MCP connections, artifact generation and multi-agent delegation, with no fee beyond usage. It puts OpenAI's internal agent-orchestration stack into direct competition with the agent-framework vendors this thread tracks. (OpenAI)
  • Salesforce completed its acquisition of Fin, folding the AI customer-service company's model suite and technical team into Salesforce AI Labs alongside Agentforce. Per Salesforce's own release, Fin serves 30,000+ companies with an average 76% autonomous resolution rate across chat, email, WhatsApp, SMS, voice and Slack, and will keep operating as a distinct product line rather than being absorbed. (Salesforce)

headline: OpenAI ships ChatGPT Images 2.5
html: • OpenAI shipped ChatGPT Images 2.5 — sharper detail, faster editing, roughly 50% lower latency, new Sketch and Templates features, and two new API models ("Flare" and "Sunburst"). A straightforward product ship rather than a thread-critical development; recorded because it led TLDR AI's third slot on 09-09 and the corpus had never mentioned it. (TLDR AI) <!-- k: t=enterprise-agent-product-race axis=late-catch -->

headline: Cognition raises over $2bn at a $48bn valuation, nearly doubling in four months
html: • Cognition raised more than $2bn in a Series E led by Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, valuing the maker of the Devin coding agent at $48bn — close to double the $26bn it carried four months ago. The company put run-rate revenue at almost $900m, up from $492m, and named Nvidia, GE Aerospace, Citi and Mercedes-Benz as production customers of the agent. ⚠️ The revenue and customer figures are the company's own, reported via Bloomberg, not independently verified. (Bloomberg)

headline: Altman apologizes for a "messy" Astra rollout that left paying Plus/Pro/Business/Enterprise users without access
html:
• Sam Altman publicly apologized for the Astra launch's staged access, which prioritized OpenAI's own Daybreak cybersecurity-tester cohort and left paying ChatGPT subscribers — including Pro subscribers, who normally get first access to new releases — watching enterprise customers go first instead. In his own words on X: "first, sorry for the messy rollout. second, when we screw up, we try to make it right. third, we should be able to begin broad rollout to API customers and chatgpt subscribers in the near future. as usual we will start with pro subscribers." OpenAI is compensating with "one banked reset for every day you don't have access to Astra on your paid ChatGPT plan," and Altman said he was hopeful (not promising) Pro subscribers could use it over the 09-05/09-06 weekend. This directly complicates this thread's own 09-03 entry, which read Astra reaching "Business and Enterprise tiers alongside Plus and Pro within days" — the "within days" promise ran into the same Daybreak-first gating that Frontier Gatekeeping already tracks as this thread's lab-run access-control pattern. (Sam Altman on X, The Verge, Unite.AI)
  • OpenAI silently changed several of GPT-6 Astra's headline benchmark figures in the hours and days after its own launch post went up, Fortune reported, rather than the independent-evaluator gap this thread already has on record. Astra's stated hallucination rate went from 4.2% (in the version live at 2:23pm ET on launch day) to 2% roughly three hours later, then back to 4.2%. On ExploitBench, the score OpenAI published for predecessor GPT-5.6 Sol changed from 5.5% to 11.5%, which OpenAI told Fortune reflects "a reasoning level that is not commercially available" for Sol — i.e., the comparison model was tested with a configuration customers cannot actually buy. On ARC-AGI-3, an embargoed draft carried 98.6%, the live blog post read 99.99%, and the Arc Prize Foundation's own "powerful harness" test scored it 99.9% against 63% on the standard harness — which explains the discrepancy in the 99.9%/99.99% figures two AI newsletters quoted on 09-04, which matched neither the 98.6% headline nor the then-known 62.7% standard-harness number. OpenAI's on-record response: "we care deeply about getting evaluations right. Most evaluations have noise within a few percentage points based on the exact checkpoint, scaffold, and eval run used in reporting," calling draft-to-final adjustment standard practice. Some outside researchers call it "benchmaxxing." This is a new axis on top of the Artificial Analysis/ARC Prize dispute already logged 09-04 — not that outsiders measured differently, but that OpenAI's own published numbers moved after the fact, and in one case a score for its own predecessor model rose on a configuration customers cannot buy. (Fortune, Startup Fortune)
  • Artificial Analysis published version 4.2 of its Intelligence Index on 09-04, an interim update it said it had "deliberately held back" through the week's launches but released because "the frontier moving so quickly in the past weeks" made it necessary: AA-Briefcase (a private agentic knowledge-work set) and Surge AI's GDP.pdf are added, the saturated GPQA Diamond is dropped, and 40% of the weighting now sits on private held-out sets, double v4.1's. On the re-weighted index Claude Fable 5.1 leads, GPT-6 Astra is second with a four-point gain over GPT-5.6 Sol (it had scored level with Sol on v4.1), and Meta is the third-ranked lab ahead of SpaceXAI, Moonshot, Z.AI and Google. AA's own note does not mention Fortune's report that OpenAI changed Astra's published figures after launch; The Decoder's reading that the overhaul was "likely in response to criticism" of the Astra scoring is The Decoder's. For the benchmark dispute this thread carries, the third-party index whose flat Astra score fed the skepticism now shows a gain — on a different test set, which is the point. (Artificial Analysis, The Decoder)

headline: OpenAI markets Astra as "the world's best computer use model," publishing benchmark numbers and pricing it into Business/Enterprise ChatGPT tiers plus Azure and AWS
html:
• OpenAI's launch materials call Astra "the world's best computer use model," citing an OSWorld 2.0 offline-subset score of 72.6% completed in roughly 40 minutes per task, against predecessor GPT-5.6 Sol's 65.7% at roughly 75 minutes per task — a claimed 47% completion-time improvement — for a model built to navigate browsers, spreadsheets, websites and desktop applications and carry out multistep agentic workflows. It reaches ChatGPT's Business and Enterprise tiers alongside Plus and Pro within days of the Thursday cybersecurity-tester-only start, plus the OpenAI API, AWS Bedrock and Microsoft Azure — priced at $10/million input and $50/million output tokens standard ($20/$100 in a 2.5x-faster "Fast" mode). (TechCrunch, VentureBeat)
  • OpenAI published a 39-page paper, "Improved Short Gaps Between Primes," proving that infinitely many consecutive primes differ by at most 186 — the paper's own introduction cites Polymath 8b's 246 from 2014 as the bound it builds past — and stating in its abstract that "the proof is due to GPT 6 Astra," with a machine-checked Lean formalization, as part of the 09-03 Astra launch materials. The method combines Polymath 8a and Stadlmann's equidistribution estimates with new factorization conditions that enlarge the support of the multidimensional Selberg sieve, establishing DHL[40,2]; mathematicians Weijie Su and Perry Metzger noted the result the same day. The third lab pure-math claim in one week alongside Anthropic's Fermat formalization, and the second launch-day Astra claim this thread carries whose checking is left to outsiders. (OpenAI — paper PDF, Weijie Su on X)

headline: Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash and Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 ship the same day, both pitched at long-horizon agentic work at workhorse prices
