On 2026-05-22, Semafor reported The Line formally halted until after 2030, with NEOM's Oxagon zone redesignated the priority — and Oxagon itself reportedly re-pivoting toward data centers, i.e. the same real estate now aimed at AI infrastructure instead of the walled linear city. (AGBI, houseofsaud.com)
  • The fiscal squeeze behind that retreat is the same one behind the AI ramp: oil near $71/barrel through mid-2025 against a ~$90+ fiscal-balance requirement, Aramco's dividend cut ~$40B for 2025, an $8B giga-project write-down at end-2024, a "close to zero" 2024 PIF investment return, and PIF cash reserves down to ~$15B — the lowest since 2020. Capital didn't expand to cover both The Line and HUMAIN; giga-project spend contracted while AI spend ramped into the same window. (houseofsaud.com)
  • HUMAIN, PIF's AI arm chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, launched 2025-05 to build the full AI stack — data centers, cloud, models, apps — consolidating existing national AI capacity including ties to Aramco/Aramco Digital. Within roughly its first eleven months it assembled a ~$21-23B named-partnership deal book: AMD $10B (confirmed via AMD's own investor-relations release — 50MW of compute live by Q4 2025, scaling to 500MW+ over five years, plus a Cisco joint venture targeting 1GW), AWS ~$5.3B (a dedicated AI Zone/AWS region in the Kingdom, online 2026), xAI $3B (a Series E participation, ~Feb 2026, making HUMAIN a minority xAI shareholder — the stake is reported to convert into SpaceX shares once xAI's merger into SpaceX completes), and AirTrunk ~$3B (an initial data-center campus with the Blackstone/CPPIB-backed operator). (ir.amd.com, TechCrunch, Argaam)
  • The xAI position is also a physical buildout, not just an equity stake: xAI and HUMAIN are building a 500MW data-center hub in Saudi Arabia — xAI's first major deployment outside the US — with an initial cluster of 18,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs, and Grok is being rolled out nationwide as what xAI's own announcement calls a "unified national AI layer" for government and private-sector use. (DataCenterDynamics, x.ai)
  • Chip access has one confirmed Saudi-specific data point: the US approved sale of up to 35,000 advanced Nvidia chips (~$1B) to HUMAIN and UAE's G42 in November 2025, reported tied to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Washington visit — a reversal of prior US resistance to direct advanced-chip exports to state-backed Gulf AI firms. A further export-control easing found this pass (2026-07-10) was UAE-only, not Saudi — flagged so it isn't mistaken for a second Saudi-specific move. (CNBC)
  • ⚠ Open reconciliation gap, not resolved this pass: board.yaml's current thrust line for PIF ("~$12.5B/yr AI run-rate — AWS $5B + AirTrunk $3B + Humain $1.2B + xAI $3B") is well below this crawl's ~$21-23B HUMAIN deal-book tally, and the board's "Humain $1.2B" line item in particular doesn't match anything found this pass — the AMD $10B deal in particular has no line on the board at all. May be an annualized-run-rate-vs-headline-total gap rather than an error, but worth a /classify pass. Two of PIF's own 2030 AUM targets ($2.67T vs. ~$1.45T, from separate PIF-adjacent announcements) also don't reconcile against each other. Full sourcing and confidence levels: artifacts/findings/pif-2026-08-04.md and artifacts/bundles/pif-2026-08-04/provenance.yaml.

headline: Ping An Bank becomes the first listed Chinese lender to adopt formal AI rules
html: • Ping An Bank became the first listed Chinese lender to formally adopt rules governing its use of artificial intelligence, after its board approved AI management measures in a Wednesday filing The Shenzhen-listed bank is part of Ping An Group; SCMP analysts expect other mainland banks to follow as regulators tighten oversight of AI use, and the full rules have not been made public. (South China Morning Post)

headline: Ping An's CTO says daily AI token use is up tenfold in a year while cost per token fell 76%
html: • Ping An's chief technology officer Ray Wang told Alibaba's Apsara Conference that the group's average daily AI token consumption rose from 30 billion at the end of last year to more than 300 billion, on roughly doubled computing capacity (800 to 1,500 petaflops), with cost per token down 76%. He said full-stack optimization raised token output per unit of computing power by 368%; that its AI-powered "Express Service" has handled over 100 million user interactions in four months with a 92% end-to-end resolution rate; that AI-generated code is about 80% of total code output; and that its AI Doctor's hallucination rate is under 0.3%. These are company-reported figures from a vendor-conference talk. (Ping An press release via PR Newswire)

sources.label: Ping An press release via PR Newswire

headline: A critical read of the H1 results: new-business growth trails peers, and an unverifiable AI health-model claim surfaces
html:
• Insurance Business Magazine's analysis of the H1 2026 results found Ping An's Q1 new-business-value (NBV) growth of 20.8% "trailed several domestic peers by a wide margin" — China Life posted 75.5%, with some peers exceeding 70%. This is the first outside-analyst pushback this thread has logged against a set of figures that, until now, have come almost entirely from Ping An's own filings and press releases.
  • The same analysis flags a new, unverifiable AI claim: Ping An says its "Medical LLM 3.5" achieved a top score on HealthBench Hard, but "public trackers...list no entry for a Ping An model," meaning the claim can't currently be checked against any public leaderboard — a different, not-yet-logged model from the PingAnGPT-Qwen3-32B/CNFinBench claim already on this thread, and a direct instance of the "flagged, not yet resolved" pattern this thread already carries (the AI Family Doctor user-count discrepancy). This is the MH-adjacent thread of Ping An's AI story getting scrutinized rather than repeated — a health-specific model claim the company has not backed with checkable evidence. (Insurance Business)

headline: The interim report refines the automation percentages, and adds two bigger numbers
html:
• Ping An's official 1H 2026 interim report restates the automation figures this thread is built on, slightly down on both: 59% of life claims settled through "quick claim" (against ~60% on file) and 94% of auto policies sold through the dealer channel intelligently issued in under a minute on average (against ~93%). The movement is noise; the point is that these are now company-filed rather than inferred. (Ping An 1H 2026 results)
  • Two figures are genuinely new and larger than anything this thread had: smart fraud detection avoided RMB 7.11bn in claims payouts, up 10.4% YoY, and AI service agents handled ~939 million interactions — 81% of all customer-service volume — in H1. An 81% share moves this from "AI assists the service desk" to "the service desk is AI, with a human exception path", which is the scale at which the NFRA framework's AI-decision liability question stops being theoretical. (Ping An 1H 2026 results)

headline: Group-level H1 results land, with an AI number of a different shape
html: • Ping An Insurance (Group) Company of China (HKEX:2318/SSE:601318, the parent) reported H1 2026 on its confirmed 08-20 date: revenue RMB 615.4bn (+12.6% YoY), net profit RMB 92.6bn (+36.1% YoY), interim dividend RMB 0.98/share. No group-level profit-share AI figure comparable to the subsidiary's 4.6%, but real activity-volume metrics: average daily token consumption exceeded 120bn in June 2026 (up from 30bn in December 2025), AI service reps handled ~939mn interactions (81% of total customer-service volume), AI-assisted sales reached RMB 57,313mn in H1, fraud-detection AI saved RMB 7.11bn in claims (+10.4% YoY), and 88% of business scenarios are now AI-enabled. (PR Newswire, Manila Times)

headline: H1 results land on the due date, with an AI number attached
html:
• Ping An Healthcare and Technology / "Ping An Good Doctor" (1833.HK) reported H1 2026 on its confirmed board-meeting date. Total revenue RMB 2.484bn; net profit attributable to shareholders RMB 219mn, +63.5% YoY; adjusted net profit RMB 227mn, +37.7%. B-end corporate health-management revenue RMB 714mn, +65.1% YoY, now 28.7% of total — the enterprise channel is where the growth is. (Sina Finance)
  • The disclosure this thread's ledger entry was explicitly holding for exists: AI contributed ~4.6% of gross profit (AI业务贡献毛利占比约4.6%), alongside 9.7mn+ cumulative AI-doctor users and AI-medical-pay network coverage at 149,000 of 245,000 partner pharmacies. A rare case of a health company putting a hard number on AI's contribution to the P&L rather than describing a strategy. (Sina Finance)
  • This is the SUBSIDIARY only. The group parent (HK:2318 / SH:601318) reports separately on 2026-08-20, now pinned by the company's own voluntary HKEX/SSE announcement filed 08-13 — closing the "group-level date unconfirmed" gap this thread carried since 08-04. Watch for a group-level AI-contribution figure to set beside the 4.6%.
  • ⚠️ Trap logged, and it is a nasty one for this issuer specifically: English-language wire mirrors (PRNewswire, Barchart) served 2026-dated URLs and headlines ("...reports strong interim results...AI fuels new growth momentum") whose BODY was the August 19 2025 H1-2025 release, prior-year numbers and all — RMB2.5bn revenue, RMB134mn profit, dateline "HONG KONG, Aug. 19, 2025." The genuine 2026 figures were reachable only via primary Chinese-language financial press. Do not accept an English wire mirror for Ping An without checking the dateline inside the body.

headline: Thread opened + crawled
html:
• Opened following a board-pass audit that found the entire insurance pocket with zero live thread coverage — Ping An was flagged in its own board gloss as "the strongest insurtech-AI angle (240M-customer ecosystem)" among the pocket's seven kingdom-rank insurers, and this crawl confirms that flag with hard, dated, primary-sourced numbers.
  • Ping An's WAIC 2026 press release (2026-07-21, fetched and confirmed directly): the Intelligent Underwriting System cut average initial underwriting review time to ~1.5 hours, doubled daily processing volume per underwriter, and raised the risk-interception rate by 16%; an "Intelligent Policy Issuance Robot" now auto-processes 93% of new vehicle-insurance policies (turnaround 6 minutes -> 1.2 minutes); Ping An P&C claims 100% AI coverage across core claims scenarios with an 80% efficiency gain. (Ping An)
  • Insurance Journal (2026-03-31): nearly 60% of accident/health claims are now automated (up from almost none five years ago), some settling in 51 seconds; AI handled 70% of Ping An Bank's RMB 500B in 2025 loan recoveries; the auto-insurance expense ratio fell 1.7 points over nine years (~RMB 5B in added underwriting profit); headcount fell 118,000+ (~30% from its 2018 peak). CTO Ray Wang: "The AI era successfully opened the window for reshaping services. The returns on investment are tangible, highly visible, and unequivocally compelling." (Insurance Journal)
  • PingAnGPT-Qwen3-32B, Ping An's self-developed financial LLM, ranked #1 on the CNFinBench leaderboard — ahead of GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4, and DeepSeek-R1 (671B) — on financial reasoning, Q&A, and compliance/risk- control metrics; deployed across 97 real business scenarios including auto-insurance claims. (Ping An, 2026-03-13)
  • China's NFRA issued sector-wide AI guidance for banking/insurance, dated 2026-06-18 (金发〔2026〕8号): explicitly covers AI in underwriting, claims, and pricing; establishes that liability for AI-assisted decisions rests with the insurer, not the algorithm; requires human- oversight mechanisms for high-risk applications and board-level AI governance. No enforcement action naming Ping An specifically has surfaced — this is the framework Ping An now operates under, the rule of the road, not evidence of scrutiny. (Sina Finance)
  • Flagged, not yet resolved: Ping An's "AI Family Doctor" user count is reported inconsistently across sources (90M monthly active users in the WAIC release vs. 12M annual users elsewhere) — worth reconciling against a single primary figure before it's cited as a headline number.

headline: Qualcomm moves its data-center memory architecture into phones
html: • Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said at Snapdragon Summit that the company is scaling HBC, the High Bandwidth Compute near-memory architecture introduced with its Dragonfly data-center roadmap, down into Snapdragon devices as a co-processor, with laptops, glasses and vehicles to follow. HBC stacks compute against memory to cut the data-movement bottleneck; the data-center versions (HBC Gen 1 on the Dragonfly AI250, rated at 133 TB/s per card, later generations on the AI300) are separate implementations, and Qualcomm says it will give details at Mobile World Congress in March 2027. It is the first sign the Dragonfly-era memory design is being reused outside the data center, alongside the Samsung and SK hynix commercialization deal logged 08-26. (Converge Digest, Gadgets Now)

headline: Qualcomm joins Cornelis Networks' open AI-rack interconnect push
html: • Qualcomm Technologies joined AI-networking startup Cornelis Networks in unveiling "Active Compute Fabric," an open rack-scale and cross-rack interconnect architecture for AI data centers, as Cornelis raised $205 million to bring it to market. The collaboration, announced at the AI Infra Summit, pairs Cornelis's programmable-fabric approach (built on open standards UALink, ESUN and Ultra Ethernet) with Qualcomm's data-center push — Tony Pialis, Qualcomm's EVP/GM of Data Center, said "moving data efficiently across the rack becomes just as important as the compute itself" as AI systems scale. It is a new named ecosystem partner for Qualcomm's Dragonfly-era data-center silicon business, alongside the already-tracked Meta, Microsoft and Amazon relationships, and reads as an explicit open-standards counter to Nvidia's proprietary NVLink. (Cornelis Networks)

headline: Amazon signs on as a second Dragonfly-era customer, and Qualcomm stock jumps ~10%
html:
• Amazon and Qualcomm announced a multi-generational collaboration on custom AI data-centre silicon, and Qualcomm's stock rose about 10% on the news. As part of the deal Qualcomm issued Amazon a warrant for up to 25 million of its own shares. ⚠️ The "$4 billion" figure in most headlines is the value of that warrant — not cash consideration, and not a disclosed contract size, a distinction most coverage collapsed. Amazon is a new named customer for the Dragonfly data-center silicon business this thread tracks, alongside Meta's already-disclosed Dragonfly C1000 relationship. (CNBC)
  • Qualcomm's 8-K discloses that the Amazon warrant vests against up to $60bn in payments, a ceiling no coverage carried. Filed today for a 09-03 event under Item 3.02, it records a warrant to Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC for up to 25,000,000 shares at $161.26, vesting in tranches tied to execution of commercial arrangements, binding purchase orders and actual purchases, capped at $60 billion in payments, with 3,750,000 shares — 15% — vesting immediately against initial purchase commitments. The widely-reported "$4bn" remains warrant value, not a contract; the $60bn is the parties' own written ceiling on the commercial relationship. (SEC 8-K)

headline: Samsung and SK hynix sign on to help build Qualcomm's memory-stacking answer to HBM
html: • Qualcomm EVP Durga Malladi said at the 2026-08-26 Deutsche Bank Technology Conference that Samsung and SK hynix have agreed to help commercialize Qualcomm's HBC (High Bandwidth Compute) architecture — which stacks LPDDR DRAM directly on top of a compute die, a near-memory alternative to HBM — after Qualcomm pitched HBC's advantages and HBM's shortcomings at its June Investor Day; Malladi said he expected pushback from the two Korean memory makers and instead got an active proposal to collaborate. Qualcomm will design the compute die and TSV integration and work with TSMC on packaging; Samsung/SK hynix handle DRAM stacking. First-generation HBC products are targeted for commercialization/shipment in 2027. HBC is one of the named components of the Dragonfly data-center portfolio (alongside the Dragonfly C1000 CPU and AI300 accelerator), so this is a concrete supply-chain commitment behind the "first silicon dates" question this thread tracks — though it is a memory-partner agreement, not silicon itself, and 2027 is later than the Sept/December contribution timing already on this thread's radar. (TrendForce, The Elec)

headline: Modular closed, Lattner installed, guidance reaffirmed not raised
html:
• The $3.9B all-stock Modular acquisition closed, and co-founder Chris Lattner — creator of LLVM, Swift and MLIR — was named to lead Qualcomm's advanced AI software effort. The anti-CUDA play is now formally staffed and closed rather than pending. Modular's Mojo language hit 1.0 on 08-11/12, two weeks after the close. (Qualcomm)
  • On the live test — did Dragonfly move guidance? No. Q3 FY26 revenue ~$9.9B, and on the call Qualcomm reaffirmed rather than raised its datacenter targets: $5B revenue in FY2027, $15B by FY2029. It did name Meta as a Dragonfly C1000 customer — an "Agentic CPU" on the Oryon architecture aimed at agent orchestration and multi-step reasoning. A named hyperscale customer without a guidance change is a real datapoint in both directions.
  • The open Ventana/RISC-V question resolves as "both, not either." Ventana's Veyron V2 custom-silicon business now has two hyperscale customers each contracted for >$1B in FY2027. Dragonfly does not supersede it.
  • First third-party software-ecosystem move around the new silicon: Multiverse Computing partnered with Qualcomm to optimise models for the AI200/AI250 accelerators, claiming 93% faster performance (08-05). Same day as the Modular close, Qualcomm also signed a 10-year BMW chip-supply deal.

headline: First named software partner for the Dragonfly accelerators
html: • Multiverse Computing and Qualcomm announced a partnership to optimize Multiverse's compressed AI models for Qualcomm's Dragonfly AI200 and AI250 accelerators (with Cloud AI100 Ultra used in demos) — aimed at letting data-center operators run more inference on existing hardware at lower power. Multiverse's Chief Sales Officer Victor Gaspar: "By combining Qualcomm's efficient AI accelerators with our model compression technology, we can deliver breakthrough improvements in performance, cost, and energy efficiency at scale." This is an ecosystem/software partnership, not a new hardware customer or a production-date update — a smaller item than the Meta/Microsoft launch-customer news, but the first named software partner since the Investor Day unveiling. (GlobeNewswire via The Globe and Mail)

sources.label: GlobeNewswire via The Globe and Mail

headline: Modular acquisition officially closed
html:
• The Modular acquisition officially closed 07-29 — resolves the thread's tracked "close expected H2-26" line. Confirmed via Qualcomm's own newsroom + 15 outlets + an SEC 8-K/10-Q filed same day. Chris Lattner (LLVM/Swift/Mojo creator) named to lead the combined "Advanced AI Software" effort. ([Qualcomm newsroom])
  • Same day, a separate 10-year BMW automotive-compute deal — auto, not datacenter; adjacent to but not core to Dragonfly's own watch.
  • Analyst price-target cuts (Baird/Bernstein/Morgan Stanley/Wells Fargo) are continued reaction to 07-29's Q3 miss, not new facts.

headline: The guide missed, but not because of Dragonfly
html:
• Q3 FY26: revenue $9.9B beat; EPS $2.21 roughly in-line. The Q4 FY26 (September-quarter) EPS guide of $2.05-2.25 missed consensus (~$2.38), driven entirely by the legacy business — memory/input-cost inflation and an accelerated Apple-modem revenue decline, now seen "materially lower" than the prior ~20% estimate. (CNBC)
  • Dragonfly did not move this guide. The two custom-silicon engagements are set to start contributing revenue in the December quarter (fiscal Q1 FY27) — the quarter after this one. (CNBC)
  • The AI story moved on a longer horizon instead: FY2029 non-handset target raised to $40B from $22B, including more than $15B in data-center revenue; HBC Gen 1 taped out, targeting a mid-2027 launch. (GuruFocus)
  • Stock fell regardless of the improved long-range story — -8% after-hours, -4.8% premarket — trading tonight's legacy-business weakness rather than 2029's promise.

headline: Investor Day: the re-entry
html: • Dragonfly C1000 CPU + AI300 accelerator launched — Meta and Microsoft named launch customers, $15B datacenter revenue by 2029 target; stock +15%. Same day: acquired Modular ($3.9B) — an explicit anti-CUDA inference-software play. Analysts frame it as the return to the market Qualcomm exited after Centriq (~2018).

headline: /29 — Tenstorrent died in two weeks
html: • The reported $8-10B Tenstorrent talks were real (06-15), then denied by Tenstorrent's CEO (06-29) — no close. Ventana's RISC-V line status unclear: superseded by Dragonfly? (open gap)

headline: Fire reported near an Aramco facility in Riyadh
html: • A large plume of smoke and fire was seen near an Aramco facility in Riyadh on Saturday, a witness told Reuters; Saudi authorities had not confirmed it and no one had claimed responsibility. It comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites have escalated. (Reuters, AFP via NAMPA)

headline: France proposes an EU release of 50 million barrels of crude and 50 million of diesel
html:
• France proposed that EU countries release 50 million barrels of crude oil and 50 million barrels of diesel, after the US asked European capitals to tap stockpiles or face a ban on US fuel exports, Politico Europe reported. Two officials said the idea is under technical assessment and Germany was reluctant; the Elysée said Macron would convene a G7 leaders' meeting as soon as possible, and a French ministry spokesperson called the proposal "rumors." (Politico Europe, CNBC)
  • G7 leaders agreed on Friday to a coordinated release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel through the International Energy Agency over four months, with a frontloaded diesel release within 20 days. The leaders' statement, published by the Elysee, says G7 members will coordinate refinery maintenance, meet in the IEA in the coming days on additional diesel releases and refrain from energy export restrictions between G7 countries; President Trump said Europe "has just agreed to release a massive amount" of diesel. (Elysee, BBC live, NBC News)
  • Brent December closed Friday at $102.25, down 6 cents, and WTI November settled at $91.11, down $1.76, after the G7 announced a 100-million-barrel release of oil and diesel. Brent had dipped under $100 before the announcement and recovered to flat on the day. (CNBC)
  • OPEC+ has delayed the capacity review that will set members' 2027 oil output quotas, with one source expecting it to finish by mid-November, Reuters reported Friday. The Iran war has delayed expansion projects and some members have yet to submit data; the group meets again Sunday. (Reuters, Egypt Oil & Gas)
  • IEA chief Fatih Birol said the agency still has ample emergency oil stocks it could release immediately if the G7's 100-million-barrel release fails to calm the market, and that reopening the Strait of Hormuz is the real fix. He spoke to reporters in Istanbul. (Türkiye Today)
  • Trump said on Friday that the US will not impose a diesel export ban, hours after the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels, calling a ban something that "was never really ever on the table". He told reporters leaving the White House that Europe's decision to tap its stockpiles was "a great thing", after saying over the previous two weeks that he supported or was weighing a ban; the Energy Secretary and oil-industry allies had warned a ban would raise pump prices. (Politico via Yahoo, Reuters via MarketScreener)

headline: Brent returns to about $100 as Trump says the US will "blow them up or make a deal"
html:
• Brent crude traded near $100 a barrel on Thursday, up about 2% from Wednesday's $98.03 settle, as President Trump said the US would "blow them up or make a deal" with Iran. Euronews had Brent up 2.6% just above $100 at about 5am ET and AP had the December contract at $99.88 at 9:35am ET; Gulf exports are back close to pre-war levels, Iran says it has received a US response, and OPEC+ is expected to hold November output targets on Sunday. (Euronews, AP via KDVR)
  • Brent's December contract settled at $102.31 a barrel on Thursday, up 4.37%, as Chinese refiners suspended October fuel exports and the Wall Street Journal reported the US is sending a third carrier group and up to 10,000 more troops to the Middle East. WTI settled at $92.87, up 2.71%; both reconcile to Wednesday's settles of $98.03 and $90.42. (Reuters via Yahoo Finance)
  • The Trump administration told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel stocks or face a possible US diesel export ban, Reuters reported Thursday, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly urged European partners to make more supplies available. Reuters cited three people close to the discussions; the US supplied about half of the EU's diesel imports in August, according to the IEA. (Reuters via Yahoo Finance Canada, CNBC)
  • Brent's December contract fell 2.6% to $99.65 a barrel and WTI fell 4% to $89.11 early Friday after Reuters reported that EU members were discussing a French proposal to release additional diesel and crude stocks. CNBC said the Reuters report rested on a single unnamed source and that it could not verify it. (CNBC, Trading Economics)
  • Putin said Russia will not supply its diesel to global markets until sanctions against Moscow are lifted, while US diesel prices sit at records above $6.50 a gallon. Speaking at the Valdai Forum he said Russia has enough diesel "but it won't reach global markets because of the bans and sanctions," that Ukraine had "partially achieved its objectives" with refinery strikes he said cost Russia 1% of GDP, and that Russia was now responding in kind; Russia this week extended its diesel export ban for fuel producers to the end of October. (Reuters via Global Banking & Finance Review)

sources.label: Reuters via Global Banking & Finance Review

headline: Brent rebounds on stalled US-Iran talks and tight US fuel stocks
html:
• Brent's more active December contract rose 2.8% to $98.81 by 10:50am ET Wednesday on stalled US-Iran talks and tight US fuel stocks, while the expiring November contract traded near $103.71. Reuters said Brent was headed for a monthly gain of about 14%, its biggest since July; EIA data showed US distillate stocks down 2.3 million barrels and gasoline down 1.7 million, and Goldman Sachs estimates Gulf exports have recovered to 23.3 million barrels a day. (Reuters via Yahoo Finance, Sharecast)
  • Brent's December contract settled up 1.9% at $98.03 on Wednesday and the expiring November contract settled at $103.50, up 91 cents, while WTI settled at $90.42 and Brent finished September about 14% higher. Oil rose on stalled US-Iran talks and tight US fuel stocks after President Trump denied reports that he was willing to give Iran sanctions relief; WTI's $1.04 gain confirms Tuesday's $89.38 settle, and OPEC+ is expected to hold November output targets on Sunday. (Reuters via CNBC, AP via BNN Bloomberg)
  • Chinese refiners have suspended exports of oil products beyond Hong Kong and Macau until further notice, and PetroChina cancelled most of its October gasoline and jet fuel cargoes, four people briefed on the matter told Reuters. The suspension runs past the Golden Week holiday to October 7 and tightens fuel markets already constrained by the Iran war; Brent rose about 2% to near $100 a barrel on Thursday as the report circulated, and CNBC said it could not independently verify it. (Reuters via MarketScreener, CNBC)
  • President Trump said at the Oval Office on Wednesday that he has not decided whether to ban US diesel exports: "I'm thinking about it." He said Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum think a ban "will help diesel, but it might raise the price of other things," and he was optimistic about prices as Hormuz flows increased; industry and some of his advisers have pushed back hard on the idea. (Politico)
  • The Trump administration told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories or face a possible US diesel export ban, three people close to the discussions told Reuters, and one source said Washington asked the EU to release 120 million barrels over six months. The European Commission, Germany, France, Italy, Britain and Ireland held a call on Thursday to discuss a release, two EU officials said, and an Elysée official said President Macron would convene a G7 leaders' video conference on fuel prices and a coordinated reserve release. (Reuters via Yahoo News)

headline: US offers 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve
html:
• The US offered to loan up to 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve on Tuesday, with WTI near $90.5 after a fall of about 2% that Reuters attributed to recovering Middle East exports rather than the loan. It is the last of the 172 million barrels ordered in March, bids are due October 6, and the reserve is projected to reach its lowest level since 1982; Reuters had Brent's November contract at $104.28 at about 1pm ET. (The National, Trading Economics)
  • Middle East crude exports rebounded to 16.3 million barrels a day in September, the highest since the war began in late February, and oil fell about 2% Tuesday as Saudi tankers resumed loading at Yanbu. Reuters's 1:03pm ET oil report put Brent (November) down $1.38, or 1.3%, at $103.88 and WTI down $2.04, or 2.16%, at $90.58, and attributed the decline to signs of recovering Middle East exports rather than to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve loan; this corrects the earlier entry that placed the fall directly after the loan offer. (Reuters via Yahoo Finance)
  • Brent's November contract settled at $102.59 and WTI at $89.38 on Tuesday, down 2.6% and 3.5%, as Middle East crude exports recovered. Brent's more actively traded December contract settled at $96.16, down 1.7%; Kpler showed September exports at 16.3 million barrels a day, the highest since the war began, and Saudi Arabia resumed loadings at Yanbu. Reuters put Brent up about 13% for the month. (Reuters via Lufkin Daily News, AP via Gorge News Center)

headline: Oil reverses off session highs on twin de-escalation signals
html:
• Brent touched $108.83 and WTI $96.54 intraday Monday before both pulled back — Brent to about $105.16 (still up 84 cents on the day) and WTI to about $92.59 — after a White House official told CNN and Axios that President Trump is open to Iran sanctions relief and releasing frozen Iranian funds for "concrete progress" on the nuclear file, landing within the same hour as reports that Saudi Arabia had restored roughly 3.5 of its East-West pipeline's 7 million barrel-per-day capacity and resumed export loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu. A US official called the indirect talks (Qatari/Pakistani mediators meeting Iran's FM Araghchi in New York Monday) "positive and constructive" and said Iran "has indicated they are flexible on the nuclear issues," but stressed gaps remain on timing and sequencing and that there is no deal "unless the nuclear issues are addressed." US equities stayed lower on the day (Dow/S&P/Nasdaq all down roughly 0.6-0.7% by early afternoon) despite the oil pullback. (CNBC, Axios, CNN)
  • Brent settled at $105.28 and WTI at $92.60 on Monday, up about 1% and 19 cents, after an early $4 spike and a dip to session lows near $96 and $91. Prices jumped when Trump rejected Iran's Hormuz plan, then eased on reports of conditional sanctions relief and Saudi pipeline flows; the Brent premium over WTI was the widest since May. (investingLive, Investrade)
  • Trump denied offering Iran sanctions relief or frozen funds in a Monday-evening post, calling the Axios report a hoax and demanding a retraction. He wrote that he "offered them NOTHING," about four hours after Axios and CNN cited US officials saying relief was possible for concrete nuclear progress; Qatari mediators were still due to meet both sides. (investingLive, Livemint)

headline: Saudi equities post the first live market read since Trump's Hormuz rejection
html:
• Saudi Arabia's Tadawul All Share Index closed Sunday's session up 0.78%, the first market of any kind to trade since Friday's US close. (Investing.com)
  • Oil futures reopened on Globex Sunday evening already pricing in the day's dueling Bessent/Trump oil claims: Brent gained roughly 1.3% to about $105.64 and WTI about 0.8% to $93.11 by shortly after 18:00 ET. The first actual price test of Saturday's Trump rejection of Iran's Hormuz plan and Iran's refusal to soften its conditions — it resolved toward continued risk-premium pricing, not a shrug. (tradingeconomics.com/oilprice.com, Bloomberg)

headline: Trump gives the first on-record US rejection of Iran's seven-day Hormuz plan
html:
• President Trump told reporters Saturday, as he boarded Marine One, that he has rejected Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz: "I reject their proposal... that deal would not be acceptable." He said Iran wants an immediate reopening only because "they're losing so badly" and is short of oil revenue under the US blockade, which he called "the greatest blockade ever in military history," and posted an image of the strait on Truth Social relabelled the "Trump Strait." The remarks are the first on-the-record US answer since Friday's Wall Street Journal report (unnamed officials) and Foreign Minister Araghchi's Friday statement that the choice "rests with the United States"; no Iranian on-record reaction to this specific rejection was found by 3:10pm ET, and oil futures do not reopen until Sunday evening. (CNN, NBC News)
  • Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran is still awaiting a "definitive" US response to its Hormuz plan through mediators and that its conditions have not changed, hours after Trump rejected the plan on the record. (Al Jazeera, CBS News)
  • Iran's rial fell to a fresh record low of roughly 2,357,000 to the dollar, extending its slide under the US blockade and sanctions campaign. (alanchand.com open-market tracker)

headline: Iran says it is "not in a hurry" for a US response to its Hormuz proposal
html:
• Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that Tehran has not yet received a US response to its seven-day Hormuz-reopening proposal and is "not in a hurry," though he said a deal would ideally come "before the midterm election." "It depends on the U.S. administration to decide," Araghchi told reporters, reiterating that Iran wants Washington to return to the terms of the June 17 memorandum of understanding that collapsed amid renewed fighting over the summer; it remains unclear how the current proposal would prevent hostilities from resuming. Oil extended its Friday fall on the diplomatic overture, with CNBC's updated report (~1:25pm ET) putting Brent down 2.3% to $104.09 and WTI down 2.5% to $92.21. (CNBC)
  • Brent settled at $104.32 a barrel Friday (down $2.28, or 2.1%) and WTI at $92.41 (down $2.20, or 2.3%), as hopes of a US-Iran path to reopening the Strait of Hormuz outweighed continuing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Thursday's settles were $106.60 and $94.61; WTI fell about 7.9% on the week (contract roll included) while Brent ended $0.45 higher. (EnergyNow, citing Reuters, Kitco PM report)
  • The Wall Street Journal reported late Friday that President Trump has rejected Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November midterms, citing unnamed US officials; Iran said it was awaiting a US response. The report came after oil had settled, so the first price reaction is Sunday evening's futures open; Washington has made no on-record response. (France 24, CNA, Reuters)
  • The EU's energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen warned EU energy ministers in a Friday letter that the bloc faces "a price crisis linking to a supply crisis" from the Iran war and asked governments to consider measures to sustain gas-storage injections or cut gas and electricity demand. He wrote that the EU is better prepared than in the winter of 2021, when Russia squeezed gas supplies, but that governments must step up preparations for this winter; Reuters saw the letter at about 3pm ET. (Reuters, via Devdiscourse)
  • Talk of a US ban on diesel exports pushed West Texas Intermediate as much as $12.02 a barrel below Brent on Thursday, the widest gap since May 6, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright has sounded out major refiners on voluntary export restraint, Reuters reported Friday. Wood Mackenzie says a ban would push about 700,000 barrels a day into storage and fill Gulf Coast inventories in just over a month; the US exports about 1.2 million barrels a day net of 5.1 million produced (Morgan Stanley), US diesel hit a record $6.528 a gallon this week, and the White House denied a 90-day ban report on Wednesday. Reuters' Friday wire also had US gasoline futures down about 4%. (Reuters, via The Business Times, Reuters, via Yahoo Finance)
  • Saudi Arabia is exporting 6 million barrels a day of crude in September, its highest since the Iran war began and back to its 2025 monthly average, Kpler data show, even with the East-West pipeline closed. The kingdom has rerouted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz along a shipping lane the US military carved out along Oman's coast; Hormuz oil flows averaged 13.2 million barrels a day over seven days to Wednesday against about 17 million before the war, and Brent has pulled back from nearly $110 after the pipeline closure as confidence grew that the outage was less disruptive than feared. (CNBC)

headline: Brent tops $105 on stalled talks and diesel-ban uncertainty
html:
• Brent crude rose about 2% to above $105 a barrel on Thursday, touching $106.50, as US-Iran talks showed little sign of progress and traders weighed a possible US ban on diesel exports. Brent was up $2.03 at $105.11 and WTI up $1.48 at $93.64 by about 9:20am ET; reports said Iran gave the US a week to meet its demands including lifting the naval blockade, a White House official on Wednesday denied a report of a 90-day diesel export ban, and the European Commission said it is concerned. These are intraday quotes. (Reuters via Yahoo Finance)
  • Brent crude jumped about 5% toward $108 a barrel on Thursday after Saudi Arabia said it intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles fired at Taif and the Yanbu area, then pared to about $105 (+2.0%) by 12:29pm ET on reports that US and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased deal to reopen Hormuz. Reuters had Brent at $105.12, up $2.04 from Wednesday's settle, and WTI at $94.15; the Houthis said they attacked Saudi military sites in Jazan, and it was not clear whether the missiles aimed at the Red Sea export route caused damage. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline has been shut since 09-11 and is being repaired. (Reuters via CNA, Reuters via The Economic Times)
  • Saudi Arabia's Red Sea export hub Yanbu had still not resumed crude tanker loadings on Thursday, two days after the East-West pipeline restarted, and a return to full capacity could take six weeks or more, Reuters reported. Crude was flowing into Red Sea coast refineries and volumes were building in the pipeline, which restarted Tuesday after the 09-11 drone attacks damaged three pumping stations; Aramco told European refiners it is still building a "critical mass" of volumes, Kpler showed about six tankers due to load 09-24 to 09-27, and the line had carried about 4 million barrels a day, roughly 4% of global supply. (Reuters via Baird Maritime)
  • Quoted war-risk insurance for Saudi-linked tankers at Yanbu has tripled to about 3% of vessel value from under 1% in early July, OilPrice reported on Thursday, citing Reuters, against up to 7% at Jizan and 6% to 9% for Hormuz voyages. That is roughly $3 million per Yanbu voyage against at least $100,000 before the war; charter rates are at least $500,000 a day, and the Houthis have threatened Saudi-linked vessels near Bab el-Mandeb without the US air support Hormuz has received. (OilPrice via Yahoo Finance)
  • Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said Thursday that any disruption to its operations can be fixed "within days" and that Aramco is studying a fourth and a fifth crude export route and more storage abroad, including in Japan. Speaking to Nikkei Asia in Tokyo, Nasser said Aramco can also use the 320km Sumed pipeline from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, that "we never stopped" supplying customers, and that barrels offered outside existing sales agreements will not return to the market "until the situation improves"; he cited the 2019 drone attack, after which operations were fully restored in 11 days. (Asharq Al-Awsat, Saudi Gazette)
  • French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday that France will send military resources — soldiers, radar systems and defense systems — to protect Saudi Arabia's Yanbu export hub, the Red Sea alternative route this map has tracked since Houthi missile attacks disrupted it. "We are going to send military resources, that is to say, soldiers, radar systems and defence systems, to protect this site — not to get us involved in any conflicts, but to protect this site," Macron said in a primetime TF1/France 2 interview, tying the commitment to surging oil prices and reassuring the French public that France has adequate winter fuel supplies. (RFI)

headline: Brent reverses its overnight dip toward $98.50 and trades near $101 as Iran answers Trump's "annihilate" threat
html:
• Brent crude reversed its overnight losses on 09-23, trading near $100 to $101 a barrel after dipping toward $98.50, a level that would have extended its losing streak to a sixth session, as Iran's military called President Trump's threat to "annihilate" it a sign of "strategic desperation." Iran's General Staff warned of strikes "more crushing" than earlier in the nearly seven-month war and Tehran laid out conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz. WTI was near $91 (November contract). ⏱ Intraday reads as of about 10am ET; no settle yet. (CNBC, Treasury yields and oil, CNBC, Iran and Hormuz)
  • Brent crude settled up $3.83, or 3.86%, at $103.08 a barrel on Wednesday, ending a five-session losing streak, while West Texas Intermediate gained $1.64, or 1.81%, to $92.16. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly Tehran would never surrender to the US but still believes in diplomacy, a day after Trump warned he could "annihilate" Iran; a senior Iranian official said differences remain in the indirect talks, and US crude inventories rose 3 million barrels to 426.4 million against an expected draw. (Reuters via Yahoo Finance)
  • A White House official told Reuters on 09-23 that a Politico report of a planned 90-day ban on US diesel exports was "fake news", and US ultra-low-sulfur diesel futures fell about 5% at the settle. Politico, citing five people, had said the administration was working on the ban despite internal disagreement and oil-industry opposition; Energy Secretary Chris Wright said earlier in the day that an export ban would not work, and Maine's two senators asked Trump to release emergency heating oil as diesel hit record prices. European diesel futures rose as much as 7% intraday. (Investing.com via Yahoo Finance, Reuters via Yahoo Finance)

headline: Brent drops toward $99 and WTI falls over 2% on Iran's Hormuz-reopening offer, a fifth straight losing session
html:
• Brent crude fell below $99 a barrel Tuesday and WTI declined more than 2%, extending a losing streak into a fifth straight session, after Reuters reported Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the US eases its blockade — Brent fell more than 3.5% off the day's high. CNBC separately reported Brent down 1.8% intraday to $98.56 and WTI down 2.3% to $93.60, citing UN General Assembly diplomatic hopes and a partial recovery in Saudi exports as compounding drivers. ⏱ Intraday Tuesday quotes; no settle price found yet. (US News, Reuters wire, CNBC)
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on 09-22 the Trump administration is examining whether a full or partial ban on US diesel exports is feasible, and President Trump said he supports one and that a decision would come quickly "one way or another." US diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon (AAA), almost $3 above a year ago, with California at $8.44; Russia already has a diesel export ban, and the American Petroleum Institute warned that restricting exports "would only compound the problem." A Dow Jones Energy analyst said a ban would help prices in the short term but hurt over the long term. (CNBC)

headline: The decline holds into Monday's US session; both benchmarks trade under $100
html:
• Brent and WTI both extended Sunday evening's decline through Monday's US session, both benchmarks' futures below $100 a barrel and November WTI down nearly 4% at $92.28 by mid-morning ET, as hopes rose for US-Iran diplomatic contact around this week's UN General Assembly. Iran's Revolutionary Guard separately warned Monday it would deploy new weapons against previously-unstruck targets if the US launched a new offensive — rhetoric that did not stop the decline. ⏱ Intraday, mid-session; no Monday settle exists yet. (Yahoo Finance)
  • Front-month WTI closed at $95.78 a barrel, down 4.5%, and Brent fell 3.5% to $100.24, a fourth straight losing session for both benchmarks, after President Trump told Fox News he would probably be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at the UN General Assembly this week, and administration officials told the New York Times he has decided against bombing Iran-allied Houthi forces in Yemen for now. Both levels reconcile against Friday's settles ($100.30 WTI, $103.87 Brent). TD Securities' Ryan McKay: "It appears that without a major escalation Iran may have lost notable leverage in the Strait" — Middle East oil flows are now around 80% of pre-war levels per JPMorgan. (CNBC)
  • Russia is set to extend its ban on most diesel exports beyond the end of September, Bloomberg reported Monday, as US diesel prices hit a fresh all-time high above $6.50 a gallon — a squeeze compounding a weekend Ukrainian strike on a major Russian oil refinery outside Moscow. Russia accounted for roughly 10% of global diesel exports before its 2022 invasion of Ukraine; the US price has nearly doubled from $3.69 a gallon a year ago. (Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance)

headline: Saudi Arabia answers the Yanbu claim for the first time: attempted and thwarted, not hit
html:
• The Saudi-led coalition said Houthi attempts on civilian infrastructure at Yanbu — where the East-West pipeline reaches the Red Sea — and at Taif, Baysh and Farasan were thwarted, and separately confirmed that a ballistic missile aimed at Riyadh was intercepted, the first time the Saudi capital has been targeted in this escalation. No further detail on the Yanbu attempt was given and no casualties or damage were reported at any site; Aramco did not respond to the Associated Press's request for comment. This is the first Saudi response of any kind to the Houthi claim of "massive fires" at Aramco's Yanbu facilities, which this thread has carried since Friday night as an unconfirmed assertion, and it points the other way. ⚠️ It remains one side's account: the AP states it could not independently verify either version, and "thwarted" is no more independently established than "hit" — what has changed is that there are now two competing accounts on the record rather than one unanswered one. What this does not touch: the East-West "Petroline" damage dates to the 09-10 drone strike and is unaffected by Saturday's attempt, so the October allocation cuts notified to European refiners rest on that older mechanism and stand unchanged. ⏱ The statement was issued late Saturday, so the event belongs to digest-day 09-19; logged here on 09-20 because it lands before the 6:00pm ET CME crude reopen and changes the supply picture that reopen prices. (AP via NPR)
  • Gulf equities, the only market open to price any of it, read it mildly. Saudi Arabia's Tadawul opened 0.5% lower and closed down 0.3% at 10,750, while Aramco's own shares reversed an early dip to close 1.3% higher.
  • CME crude, which reopened at 6:00pm ET Sunday, fell through the Asian session rather than pricing in the weekend's Houthi claims, with Brent's November contract at $101.75/bbl and WTI's October contract at $98.34/bbl as of 0859 GMT (4:59am ET) — each roughly 2% lower and the weakest levels since 09-10. The move came with a concrete supply data point behind it: satellite data JPMorgan cited showed Saudi crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaging 2.9 million barrels per day over the prior six days, up sharply from 700,000 bpd in August — actual-barrels evidence for the reroute this thread has tracked through Aramco's own ship-to-ship-transfer announcements, now with a number attached. ⏱ Intraday Globex quotes during the reopen session, not a settle. (TradingPedia, citing Reuters/JPMorgan)

headline: The first market read on the Yanbu claim: Aramco closes higher
html: • Saudi Arabia's Tadawul index opened 0.5% lower on the first trading session after the Houthis claimed strikes on Riyadh and on Aramco's Yanbu facilities, then pared the loss to close 0.3% down at 10,750 — while Saudi Aramco's own shares reversed an early 0.6% fall to finish 1.3% higher. ACWA Power was the steepest faller at -2.8%. Across the Gulf: Qatar -1.1% to 9,550 (Industries Qatar -4.1%), Egypt -0.2% to 55,371, Bahrain -0.2% to 1,920, Oman -0.3% to 7,580, Kuwait -0.7% to 9,182. Gulf bourses are the only equity markets open on a Sunday, so this is the first price anywhere to incorporate the claim. The informative part is Aramco closing up on a day its own export infrastructure was publicly named as a target: the market closest to the event, and best placed to know, priced the claim as largely immaterial. That bears on the claim's credibility — neither Saudi Arabia nor Aramco has confirmed any damage at Yanbu — without settling it. ⏱ CME crude does not reopen until 6:00pm ET Sunday, so Friday's settles (Brent $103.87, WTI $100.30) remain the last traded levels and no oil price has yet responded. (Reuters, via syndication)

headline: Aramco cuts October crude to Europe as the Houthis claim a hit on Yanbu
html:
• Yemen's Houthis claimed Friday night's strikes near Riyadh's main airport and a separate hit on Saudi Aramco's Yanbu export hub, the Red Sea terminal carrying the kingdom's rerouted crude. The Riyadh alerts, blasts and fuel-depot fire themselves happened Friday night Eastern time and are recorded on 09-18; Saturday's new facts are the claim and the Yanbu target, which Saudi authorities have not confirmed. Yanbu is where East-West pipeline barrels reach the Red Sea, so a hit there bears directly on the export route this thread tracks. (NBC News/Reuters, TASS)
  • Aramco separately notified at least two European refiners they will receive no October crude under existing long-term contracts, Bloomberg reported Saturday, converting this thread's nine-day-old East-West pipeline outage into an actual loss of exportable barrels rather than a rerouting story. The notifications rest on the same "Petroline" pipeline outage this thread has tracked since the 09-10 drone strike — still not restored to full capacity despite the partial-restart plan logged here 09-17 — and extend Reuters' 09-15 report that September-loading Yanbu cargoes were already being canceled. Poland's Orlen has issued more than ten tenders for North Sea replacement barrels since; European OECD countries imported roughly 577,000 barrels/day of Saudi crude in June (IEA), the scale of trade now exposed. Oil futures are shut until Sunday evening's CME Globex reopen. (GreekReporter, citing Bloomberg, Middle East Monitor)

headline: Brent round-trips within a single session as fresh Saudi-Houthi border clashes revive the war-risk premium the pipeline restart had been paring back
html: • Brent extended Thursday's decline to a fourth straight down session in Asian trading, easing 2.2% to about $102.57 (WTI 1.9% to about $100.05), before both benchmarks round-tripped back toward flat during the US session as Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis traded fresh cross-border attacks Thursday. By midday Friday the same live CNBC page this thread has cited all week showed Brent at $104.34 (down just 48 cents on the day) and WTI at $101.66 (down 25 cents) — the Asian-session decline was real, but it did not hold once the border-clash headlines landed. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline restart plan and Oman ship-to-ship workaround (both logged 09-17) are still the supply-side story that had been removing this thread's tracked war-risk premium; Thursday's border exchange is pulling the same barrel the other way within the same 24-hour window, a clean real-time test of which force the market currently weights more. By the close, the midday "round-tripped to flat" read had not held — both benchmarks resumed their decline into Friday's settle, Brent to $103.87 (-0.91%) and WTI to $100.30 (-1.58%), each a third straight down close. CNBC's own oil page and Reuters/MarketWatch all 403'd direct fetch at finalize (a broader block than the single-page 403 logged mid-pass); the settle figures are cross-checked across tradingeconomics.com's commodity pages against two independent same-day recap sources (vittarthi.com, KBL Destinations) rather than a single wire's "settled at" sentence. (CNBC, Vantage Markets, Bloomberg, tradingeconomics.com/commodity/brent-crude-oil, tradingeconomics.com/commodity/crude-oil)

headline: Brent swings as low as ~$102 before settling at $104.82 as Saudi Arabia announces a concrete partial-restart plan for the East-West pipeline and reroutes crude through Hormuz-adjacent ship-to-ship transfers
html: • Brent traded as much as 3.6% lower, near $102/bbl, Thursday — its sharpest intraday swing in this thread's recent record — before settling down about 1% at $104.82 (WTI $101.91), as Saudi Arabia moved from the "no restart timeline disclosed" state this thread has tracked since 09-14 to a concrete plan: resuming roughly half the East-West pipeline's 7 million bpd capacity "within days," full capacity within about six weeks, while bypassing the damaged section. Aramco is separately making additional crude cargoes available to Asian refiners via ship-to-ship transfers just outside Hormuz near Oman's Sohar port — using the chokepoint the pipeline exists to avoid as a stopgap workaround for the pipeline's own outage, worth holding against this thread's running theme that both the strait and its workaround have now each been disrupted in this war. Aramco previously restored this same pipeline to full capacity within days after an April 2026 attack, a precedent this outage (nine days old at this restart announcement, since the 09-10 drone strike) has already exceeded once. (Bloomberg, Bloomberg, CNBC)

headline: Brent eases on an inventory build even as the pipeline stays shut with no restart date
html: • Brent fell about 1% to $107.64 Wednesday as reported US crude-inventory increases outweighed the still-unresolved Saudi East-West pipeline shutdown (offline since the drone strike, no restart timeline despite Tuesday's "soon" comment from the US Energy Secretary) and intensifying Saudi-backed counter-strikes against Houthi positions near Bab al-Mandeb. Two forces are pulling the same barrel in opposite directions — a bearish inventory print against a still-live chokepoint disruption on a route now carrying roughly 8x more Saudi export volume since Hormuz risk forced the reroute. (CNBC, Washington Times)

headline: Brent consolidates near $107-108 as the pipeline stays shut and Washington predicts a restart "soon" with no date given
html:
• Brent held in the $107-108 range Tuesday, near but not clearly above Monday's four-month intraday levels — sources disagree on the exact prior-close figure this pass (tradingeconomics reads Monday's close at $105.68, a separate feed puts Monday's high at $108.34), so this entry states the range rather than a reconciled percentage move. The East-West pipeline remains offline five days after the 09-10 drone attack, with no Aramco damage assessment or repair timeline yet disclosed. (TradingEconomics)
  • US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the pipeline is expected to restart "soon" — the first US official comment on a restart timeline since the shutdown — but gave no date, leaving this thread's own "no repair timeline disclosed" read from 09-14 still standing as of this pass. (Briefs.co)
  • Brent and WTI settled Tuesday at $108 and $105 respectively, holding their gains into the close rather than fading — the first full-day settle this thread has for 09-15, confirming the range this pass's earlier intraday read only approximated. A WebSearch AI summary this pass surfaced a false claim that the pipeline was "back to full capacity at 7 million bpd as of September 15"; checked directly against oilprice.com, which confirms the pipeline remains shut with no reconciled restart date — the claim traced to an unrelated April 2026 restoration after an earlier, separate attack, conflated by the summarizer with the current outage. No change to the pipeline's status from this thread's own 09-14 read. (Yahoo Finance)

headline: Brent tops $108, a four-month high, as the Saudi pipeline workaround stays shut and the Hormuz talks collapse instead of landing
html:
• Brent traded as high as $108.04 (+3.28%) and held around $106.69-108 through Monday, its strongest level in four months, extending last week's 9%+ rally rather than reversing it. The move stacks three inputs this thread and iran-conflict-widening have been tracking separately onto one session: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline — its principal workaround for avoiding the Strait of Hormuz, moving 4-5% of global crude supply — remains shut four days after the 09-10 drone attack traced to Iraq's Maysan province; the Houthis' completed hold on both Bab el-Mandeb shipping lanes (already on this thread's 09-11 record) is unresolved; and Monday's planned Salalah talks on a Hormuz shipping corridor were postponed with no new date (full diplomatic detail on iran-conflict-widening). (FinanceFeeds, EnergyNow, CNBC)
  • Unlike the 09-11 pullback this thread logged on profit-taking, this leg is not reversing — the pipeline outage is the mechanism, and it has now run four days with no repair timeline disclosed (Saudi Arabia has given no damage assessment; a comparable April attack on the same pipeline was repaired within three days, a precedent this outage has already exceeded). This is the first time in the war that Saudi Arabia's own Hormuz-avoidance route, not just the strait itself, has been the thing taken offline — pushing the "workaround" itself into the same risk category as the chokepoint it was built to avoid.

headline: the Sunday-evening reopening print the prior digest could only anticipate
html: • Brent jumped $3.62 to $108.23/bbl and WTI rose $3.15 to $103.20/bbl — a 3%+ move — when CME Globex oil futures reopened for the week at 6:00pm ET Sunday 09-13, on continued vessel attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and Monday's planned Oman Hormuz-shipping talks being reported as postponed before the reopen even printed. The reopening was the risk flagged beforehand — "oil futures reopen this evening... the risk that reopening will have to price, not something already reflected in these levels." This is the first real number behind that anticipated move, and the direct predecessor to the following day's Brent-above-$108 entry above — the same rally continuing, not two separate moves. (investinglive.com)

headline: Bab el-Mandeb is now fully Houthi-held on both shipping lanes, yet oil gave back Thursday's spike on profit-taking rather than de-escalation
html:
• The Houthis' seizure of Perim Island completed their hold on the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coast, putting both shipping lanes of the Bab el-Mandeb strait — roughly 12–15% of global maritime trade — under one combatant's control for the first time in this war; oil nonetheless fell rather than spiked, with Brent down 3.58% to $103.78 and WTI down 2.17% to $99.23, snapping five and eight consecutive days of gains respectively. Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid attributed the pullback specifically to a WSJ report that White House advisers have discussed the Iran conflict extending beyond Trump's current term — a longer war read by the market as a lower near-term disruption probability, the opposite of how the same fact reads on the conflict side. The week is still up 8–9%. See yemen-civil-war for the ground-war account of the same advance. (CNBC)
  • ✅ This thread's own open "since when" flag is resolved: Thursday's break above $100 was the first time since mid-May, not July as an earlier reading had it — stated directly in CNBC's Friday piece, not inferred, closing the discrepancy this thread has carried unresolved since 09-09. (CNBC)
  • ⚠️ Saudi Arabia's own oil output has fallen to its lowest level since 1990, per Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid, cited as one of Thursday's specific escalation inputs alongside the Houthi capture of Mokha — distinct from the US-Iran naval exchange this thread has tracked as the primary mechanism. Single-sourced to a bank strategist quoted in a market wrap, not independently corroborated. (CNBC)

headline: Brent tops $106 and WTI tops $101 by afternoon as two chokepoints — Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb — get priced at once
html:
• Brent traded $104.80–$105.07 (+3.50% to +3.81%) as of ~10:15 ET, measured from a $101.21–$101.26 prior close, while WTI reached $99.63 (+3.73%, +$3.58) from a $96.05 prior close as of 10:17 ET. Both prior closes match CNBC's own report of Tuesday 09-09's official settles — Brent at $101.21 (+3.36%) and WTI at $96.05 (+3.25%) — so the 09-09 close and today's intraday reading agree within rounding. This is a fresh leg higher on top of this thread's own 09-09 entry, which logged Brent crossing $100 intraday at $101.44. Both legs were genuinely cross-checked across three independent sources — oilprice.com, investing.com and CNBC's settle report — rather than the single-source reads this thread has had to catch and correct before. (oilprice.com, investing.com Brent, investing.com WTI)
  • ⚠️ Unresolved: this thread's own 09-09 entry says Brent crossed $100 "for the first time since July," but a separate report described the same crossing as the first since May, and today's WTI move above $99 is itself framed elsewhere as its highest "since roughly May." The level itself is not in doubt — it reconciles cleanly against its prior close above — only the how-long-since framing is unreconciled between the two readings. Needs a check against a dated historical settle series; not resolved.
  • By mid-afternoon Brent had climbed further to $106.83 (+5.55%) and WTI to $101.57 (+5.75%) — a second leg up on the morning's own $105/$99 reading, logged above in this same block. The move now reflects two chokepoints being priced at once rather than one: Hormuz, off the US-vs-Iranian-Navy tanker exchange already on this thread's 09-09 record, and Bab el-Mandeb, off a new Houthi advance past Mokha to the Hanish Islands — see yemen-civil-war for the ground-war account of the same advance. Houthi forces are pushing toward the peninsula overlooking Perim Island and Bab el-Mandeb itself, per Maritime Executive, which would give them leverage over roughly 8.1 million barrels a day transiting the strait — about 8% of global oil supply on Q2 2026 figures. A sustained disruption there forces Asia–Europe shipping around the Cape of Good Hope. The internationally recognised Yemeni government still holds the coastline and islands overlooking the shipping channels in that specific area as of the same report, and the Houthis deny that blocking traffic is their objective, saying they can already control it from positions they hold now. (Maritime Executive)

headline: The US disables five Iranian tankers, Iran hits back at Jordan, and Brent crosses $100 for the first time since July
html:
• The US disabled five Iranian tankers — M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1 and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, and M/T Derya near Kharg Island — on 09-08/09-09, after CENTCOM said the IRGC "sought to target a US warship twice" in the prior two days; crews were ordered to abandon ship before the strikes. This is the war's most direct US-vs-Iranian-Navy exchange yet, hitting tankers rather than sinking them, in a single coordinated operation rather than the one-off interdictions this thread has logged since the blockade began. (Al Jazeera)
  • Iran retaliated by attacking ten ships near the Strait of Hormuz and firing missiles at Al-Azraq base in Jordan — 18 of 20 intercepted, no casualties — while the IRGC separately claimed hits on two US destroyers (DDG-119, DDG-53), a claim CENTCOM explicitly denied as "completely FALSE." Secretary of State Rubio: "for every time they do that... they're going to lose tankers." The Jordan strike is the first time this thread has logged Iran hitting a named US-aligned state's territory directly in response to a tanker operation, rather than answering in the strait itself. (Al Jazeera, NBC News, US News)
  • Brent crossed $100 a barrel for the first time since July, trading to $101.44 (+3.6%, +$3.52) against a $97.92 prior close, cross-checked between oilprice.com and TradingEconomics as of 13:09 ET. WTI was not independently re-pulled this cut and needs a same-day check next pass. The target set is the point again, in a different register from the Aramco/Jazan strikes this thread has tracked all war: this time the target was Iranian naval assets and a treaty ally's air base, not shipping or refining infrastructure — a step from an economic war onto a state-vs-state one. (oilprice.com, TradingEconomics)

headline: Houthi strikes on Aramco, an air base and four Saudi cities push Brent to about $98.6 as OPEC+ holds October output flat
html:
• Brent traded around $98.6, up about 1.5% from Monday's close near $97.16, and WTI reached $93.64, up 2.36% from Friday's $91.48, after Houthi drones and ballistic missiles struck Saudi Aramco energy facilities, King Khalid Air Base and four Saudi cities overnight, wounding at least 73. The target set is the point: Saudi Arabia has been routing crude west to the Red Sea specifically to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, and the Red Sea coast is what was hit. ⚠️ Figures revised at 15:00 ET from an earlier "$98.14, up 1.93% from Friday's $96.28": Brent's prior close is Monday's, not Friday's, because ICE traded through Labor Day while NYMEX was shut, so WTI's Friday basis was right and Brent's was not. Cross-checked between oilprice.com's front-month contract and TradingEconomics. (Al Jazeera)
  • OPEC+ left October output unchanged, declining to add barrels against a risk premium that has taken Brent within $2 of $100 — the steady-as-she-goes stance one outlet framed as OPEC+ having "lost control of the oil market." ⚠️ The decision was reported Sunday 09-06 and recirculated today for its interaction with today's strike, not as a fresh decision. (Reuters)
  • Qatar said reopening the Strait of Hormuz "unconditionally" is a priority and is discussing new proposals with Beijing, as the US-Iran war passes six months. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Ibrahim Al Hashmi called the current "no war, no peace" state unacceptable; Qatar's prime minister raised the closure directly with Wang Yi in Beijing, and Al Hashmi separately condemned the Houthi strikes on Saudi civilian sites — Doha treating Yemen and Hormuz as one shipping file rather than two. (Al Jazeera)
  • The overnight Houthi target set is now specific, and it includes a military base as well as energy infrastructure. Dozens of ballistic missiles and drones hit Abha Airport, King Khalid Air Base, the roughly 400,000 bpd Jazan refinery, an Aramco fuel terminal and a Najran fuel terminal, igniting fires that temporarily suspended operations at the facilities struck and wounding 73. The morning entry had "Aramco energy facilities and four Saudi cities"; the air base is the addition, and it makes this a strike on Saudi military as well as export capacity. (Washington Post, CNN)
  • ⚠️ Correction to this morning's entry: Brent's move was measured from the wrong prior close. The 10:00 entry gave Brent at $98.14, "up 1.93% from Friday's $96.28." ICE Brent trades on US public holidays and closed Monday near $97.16, so Friday was never the right basis — the correct read is Brent at $98.56–98.65 intraday, up about $1.5 or 1.5%, from a Monday close near $97.16, cross-checked between oilprice.com's front-month Nov contract (98.56, +1.56, 14:09 ET, day range 96.78–99.46) and TradingEconomics (98.65, +1.49, +1.54%, prior close 97.16). WTI's basis was correct at $91.48, because NYMEX was shut for Labor Day while ICE was not — the error was applying WTI's holiday to Brent. This map's own 09-07 entry already carried Brent at $97.73 on Monday, so the contradicting figure was in the record when the morning entry was written.

headline: Aramco's Jizan refinery hit again as Brent reaches a six-week high
html:
• Saudi Aramco oil facilities were struck in fresh attacks on Monday 09-07, with the 400,000-barrel-a-day Jizan refinery hit again, and Brent rose 1.5% to $97.73 a barrel — as high as $97.93, its strongest since 23 July — while WTI climbed 1.8% to $93.10. Jizan is a Red Sea refining hub, which is the point: Saudi Arabia has been routing more crude west precisely to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, so a strike there hits the workaround rather than the chokepoint. ⚠️ Attribution is not established — Aramco had not commented on the latest damage at this cut and no group had been confirmed responsible; the Houthis claimed the July and 08-09 strikes on the same refinery, both already on this map. (CNBC, 14:52Z, OilPrice, FT, via CNBC's citation)
  • Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said on 09-07 that Tehran will declare a new "restricted zone" beginning at the line of the US naval blockade, extending toward the Strait of Hormuz and continuing into the Persian Gulf, and that "any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list." No boundaries were published — Rezaei said they would follow over "coming days and weeks" — and Al Jazeera's own explainer quotes Stephen Zunes doubting Iran can enforce the zone militarily and reading it partly as leverage over an emerging Iran-Oman shipping-corridor arrangement. Shipping data over the same week put Hormuz transits at 6-10 vessels a day against a pre-war baseline near 130. ⚠️ Announced-not-defined: this is a declaratory claim with no published coordinates and no enforcement action yet observed, and it is filed as such. (Al Jazeera, CBS News live updates)
  • Goldman Sachs said crude could reach $120 a barrel if attacks on Middle East shipping intensify, while keeping its base case a wide $80-120 range depending on whether Gulf exports normalise or the disruption broadens. Commodities co-head Daan Struyven said "events over the last few days do suggest that the risk of shipping disruptions broadening and intensifying is an important one," and the bank recommended natural gas and diesel as the cheaper hedges. (Bloomberg via BOE Report, Seeking Alpha)
  • Brent's Friday 09-04 settlement was $96.28, not the $92.68 this map carried from the 09-04 run through today — a digit transposition that reached four digests, this thread, an interpretation sidecar and the public site. The percentages recorded alongside the level were always the disproof and were never checked against it: +0.8% on the day and +7.6-7.8% on the week reconcile with $96.28 (09-03 settle $95.52, 08-28 settle $89.31) and would be -3.0% and +3.8% from $92.68. Worse, when the map's own secondary sources reported $95-97 on 09-03 and 09-04, a note was written declaring the transposed settlement authoritative and dismissing those correct reads as "intraday or contract-mismatched." WTI's $91.48 and +10% week were transcribed correctly throughout, so only the Brent level was affected. Verified against two independent instruments.

headline: TankerTrackers puts August Middle East crude exports 39% below the pre-war baseline, a 7.2 mb/d deficit down from 12.4 in May, with Iran's 1.68 mb/d expected to stay at zero
html: • Middle East crude exports in August ran 39% below the January–February baseline of 18.5 million barrels a day, a deficit of 7.2 mb/d down from 12.4 mb/d in May, according to TankerTrackers, which said on Sunday that "most may recover in the coming months" but that Iran's own 1.68 mb/d baseline "may likely remain at zero for the foreseeable future, depending on any agreement." The US military says about 90 commercial vessels have been redirected under the blockade; Iranian officials confirm no crude has passed the US warships but say up to 90 million barrels moved during the July window and that floating storage outside the line is still being sold to China at a discount — a stock Bessent put at roughly 30 million barrels remaining. With the deficit shrinking as Gulf transits recover under US escort, the supply story Tuesday's open will price is a narrowing regional gap with an Iranian zero inside it, rather than a widening one. (Al Jazeera, carrying TankerTrackers and Bessent)

sources.label: Al Jazeera, carrying TankerTrackers and Bessent

headline: CENTCOM disables two IRGC crude carriers off Kharg Island and Jask and destroys a third, with oil markets closed until Tuesday
html: • US Central Command said it permanently disabled the IRGC-linked crude carriers M/T Downy off Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask and completely destroyed the unladen carrier M/T Kylo (also known as Noxen) in the Gulf of Oman on 09-05, after the IRGC fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer that "successfully evaded" them. The strikes hit "critical components" to render the vessels inoperable rather than sink them, limiting spill risk; no casualties were reported on either side. Kharg Island handles roughly 90% of Iran's crude exports, and the Downy was struck in its waters — the first US strike on Iranian tanker infrastructure at the export terminal itself rather than on shadow-fleet vessels in transit, on a Saturday with Brent's last settlement at $96.28 (+7.6% on the week, Reuters) and no US session until Tuesday 09-08 because of Labor Day. (CNN, via KVIA, AP, via KSAT)

headline: South Korea prepares a naval deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, reversing its wait-for-the-war-to-end position
html:
• South Korea's Defense Ministry said it is making "concrete preparations" to send forces to the Strait of Hormuz — a maritime patrol aircraft, a logistics support ship, and/or a mine-detection/clearance unit are under consideration, with a parliamentary consent motion expected this month and dispatch targeted before year-end. This reverses Seoul's earlier stance of deploying only after the US-Iran war ends; officials are coordinating scale and nature of the contribution with the US, UK and France. The trigger is explicit: Trump said in August he scaled back joint US-South Korea exercises partly because Seoul had declined to help in the Iran war. The Blue House pushed back on reports that a final decision has been made, calling that framing "different from the facts" — so this is preparation and diplomatic coordination, not a confirmed deployment. This is the second US ally (after the EU, logged above under iran-conflict-widening) drawn into the campaign's military or financial machinery within the same 24 hours. (Bloomberg, via Political Wire, Free Malaysia Today)
  • Hours after reports that South Korea was making "concrete preparations" for a Hormuz deployment, a South Korean presidential official told Al-Monitor "nothing has been decided" and specifically denied the two most concrete claims in that reporting — that a deployment before year-end was settled, and that a parliamentary consent motion would be sought "this month." The official said Seoul still has to clear domestic legal procedure, assess military readiness on the Korean Peninsula, and secure National Assembly approval before any decision, and that President Lee Jae-myung might raise the question with Macron the following week — no decision date given. This sharpens the Blue House's earlier "different from the facts" pushback into specific denials: what stands is preparation and review, not an in-motion deployment timeline. (Al-Monitor)
  • Brent crude closed Friday at $96.28/bbl (+0.8% on the day, +7.6% for the week) and WTI at $91.48 (+10% for the week), while the US national average diesel price hit an all-time record of $5.85/gallon per AAA data. The move is attributed to the intensified US-Iran exchange (the Larak Island/Kuhestak strikes and the Jordan/UAE retaliation), Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and continued Hormuz transit collapse — only 4 vessels transited Thursday against a ~15/day average. Layered onto this the same week: a Houthi ground offensive launched 09-03/04 in western Yemen pushed toward the port of Mokha and hills overlooking Bab al-Mandab strait, with a wire-sourced toll climbing past 120 (AFP, Arab News) and to 129 (Gulf News) killed by Friday, including a missile strike on a restaurant in al-Makha with civilian casualties; government forces claimed recapture of some hills same day. Houthi officials separately renewed threats to close Bab al-Mandab if Gulf states join the war. ⚠️ Corrected 2026-09-07. This entry read $92.68 for Brent's Friday settle from 09-04 until today; the correct figure is $96.28 — $92.68 was a digit transposition. The note that stood here resolved the contradiction the wrong way: it declared the transposed settlement authoritative and dismissed the $95-97 secondary reads carried for 09-03 and 09-04 as "intraday or contract-mismatched." Those reads were correct. The tell was already on the page — the +0.8% day and +7.6% week changes recorded alongside the level reconcile with $96.28 (09-03 $95.52, 08-28 $89.31) and would be -3.0% and +3.8% from $92.68. WTI's $91.48 and +10% week were transcribed correctly throughout, so only the Brent level was affected. (Yahoo Finance/Reuters, OilPrice.com, Arab News, Al Jazeera, Gulf News)

headline: Brent whipsaws between $95 and $99 as Washington's barrel-volume claims keep outrunning independent ship counts
html:
• Brent closed above $95 on Wednesday (09-02) for the first time since late July, then spiked to roughly $99.38 by 8am ET Thursday (09-03, +3.4% on the day) before easing back to around $95 by afternoon trading (-0.4% net), snapping the three-session rally this thread has tracked since the 08-30/31 Larak Island strike — the intraday swing reflects markets weighing the fresh Kuwait/UAE strikes (iran-conflict-widening, above) against renewed claims that Hormuz transit volumes are recovering. (Fortune, TradingEconomics)
